entry.sum: A conformal map is a bijective holomorphic map between open sets of the plane; near each point it acts like multiplication by the nonzero number $f'(z_0)$, so it rotates and scales infinitesimal pictures and preserves angles. The Riemann mapping theorem says that every simply connected open set other than $\mathbb{C}$ itself is conformally equivalent to the unit disc $\mathbb{D}$.
key: \Omega \subsetneq \mathbb{C} \text{ simply connected},\ z_0 \in \Omega \;\Longrightarrow\; \exists!\, F:\Omega \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathbb{D},\ F(z_0)=0,\ F'(z_0)>0
\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{D}) = \Big\{\, z \mapsto e^{i\theta}\,\frac{\alpha - z}{1-\overline{\alpha}z} \;:\; \theta \in \mathbb{R},\ |\alpha|<1 \Big\}
\text{Cayley map: } z \mapsto \frac{i-z}{i+z} \text{ sends } \{\operatorname{Im} z>0\} \text{ onto } \mathbb{D}
entry.why: Conformal maps transport harmonic functions to harmonic functions, so a Dirichlet problem or a two-dimensional flow or electrostatics problem on an awkward region can be moved to the disc or half-plane, solved there, and moved back.

links.note: Because a harmonic function composed with a conformal map is again harmonic, conformal maps reduce Laplace's equation on a simply connected region to the same problem on the disc, where the Poisson integral solves it.

Two-dimensional ideal fluid flow and electrostatics are described by harmonic potentials, and classical aerofoil calculations use the Joukowski map to turn flow past a disc into flow past a wing profile.

blocks.body:
Draw two curves crossing at a point, apply the map $z \mapsto e^z$, and the image curves cross at exactly the same angle. This is no accident: a holomorphic function with nonzero derivative preserves angles between curves. A bijective holomorphic map is therefore a way of redrawing one region of the plane as another while keeping all the local geometry of angles intact.

The natural question is which regions can be redrawn as which. The answer, the Riemann mapping theorem, is startling: a square, a half-plane, a slit plane, the inside of any wiggly Jordan curve, are all conformally the same as the unit disc. This page builds the tools (Möbius maps, the Schwarz lemma) and then proves the theorem, assuming [[holomorphic]] functions and the [[arzela-ascoli]] theorem.

blocks.title: Why holomorphic maps preserve angles
blocks.body:
Near a point $z_0$ a holomorphic function satisfies $f(z_0+h) \approx f(z_0) + f'(z_0)\,h$. If $f'(z_0) = re^{i\varphi}$ with $r>0$, multiplying a small displacement $h$ by $f'(z_0)$ stretches it by $r$ and rotates it by $\varphi$. Every direction is rotated by the same angle, so the angle between two curves through $z_0$ is unchanged, and so is its orientation.

Contrast $f(z)=z^2$ at $0$, where $f'(0)=0$. The rays $\arg z = 0$ and $\arg z = \pi/4$ go to the rays $\arg w = 0$ and $\arg w = \pi/2$: the angle doubles. Angles are preserved at points where $f' \neq 0$; at a zero of $f'$ of order $k-1$ they are multiplied by $k$. Complex conjugation $z \mapsto \bar z$ preserves the size of angles but reverses their orientation; it is not holomorphic and is not called conformal here.

A useful companion fact: if $u$ is a real function of two variables and $f$ is holomorphic, then $\Delta(u \circ f) = |f'|^2 \,(\Delta u)\circ f$. In particular a harmonic function composed with a conformal map is harmonic, which is why these maps are a standard tool for Laplace's equation.

blocks.title: Conformal map
blocks.body:
Let $U, V \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be open. A conformal map (or biholomorphism) $f: U \to V$ is a bijective holomorphic map. If one exists, $U$ and $V$ are conformally equivalent. An automorphism of $U$ is a conformal map $U \to U$; they form a group $\operatorname{Aut}(U)$ under composition.

Conformally equivalent regions are indistinguishable for complex analysis: holomorphic functions on one correspond exactly to holomorphic functions on the other.

blocks.title: Injective holomorphic maps
blocks.body: If $f: U \to \mathbb{C}$ is holomorphic and injective, then $f'(z) \neq 0$ for every $z \in U$, the image $V=f(U)$ is open, and the inverse $f^{-1}: V \to U$ is holomorphic. So an injective holomorphic map is automatically a conformal map onto its image.

blocks.title: Möbius maps: the half-plane and the disc
blocks.body:
A Möbius transformation is $T(z) = \dfrac{az+b}{cz+d}$ with $ad-bc \neq 0$. It is a bijection of the Riemann sphere $\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$, it is generated by translations, rotation-dilations $z\mapsto az$ and the inversion $z \mapsto 1/z$, and it sends circles and lines to circles and lines.

The most useful example is the Cayley map $F(z) = \dfrac{i-z}{i+z}$. For a point $z$, $|F(z)|<1$ means $|z-i| < |z+i|$: $z$ is closer to $i$ than to $-i$, which is exactly the condition $\operatorname{Im} z > 0$. So $F$ maps the upper half-plane $\mathbb{H}$ onto $\mathbb{D}$, and the real axis onto the unit circle minus the point $-1$. Its inverse is $G(w) = i\,\dfrac{1-w}{1+w}$.

Inside the disc, the key maps are the Blaschke factors
$$\psi_\alpha(z) = \frac{\alpha - z}{1 - \overline{\alpha} z}, \qquad |\alpha|<1.$$
A direct expansion gives $|1-\overline{\alpha}z|^2 - |\alpha - z|^2 = (1-|\alpha|^2)(1-|z|^2)$, so $|\psi_\alpha(z)|<1$ when $|z|<1$ and $|\psi_\alpha(z)|=1$ when $|z|=1$. Also $\psi_\alpha(0)=\alpha$, $\psi_\alpha(\alpha)=0$, and $\psi_\alpha \circ \psi_\alpha = \mathrm{id}$, so $\psi_\alpha$ is an automorphism of $\mathbb{D}$ that swaps $0$ and $\alpha$. Differentiating, $\psi_\alpha'(z) = \dfrac{|\alpha|^2-1}{(1-\overline{\alpha}z)^2}$.

blocks.title: Schwarz lemma
blocks.body: Let $f: \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{D}$ be holomorphic with $f(0)=0$. Then $|f(z)| \le |z|$ for all $z \in \mathbb{D}$ and $|f'(0)| \le 1$. If $|f(z_0)|=|z_0|$ for some $z_0 \neq 0$, or if $|f'(0)|=1$, then $f(z) = e^{i\theta} z$ is a rotation.

Since $f(0)=0$, the function $g(z) = f(z)/z$ (with $g(0)=f'(0)$) is holomorphic on $\mathbb{D}$. On the circle $|z|=r<1$ we have $|g(z)| \le 1/r$, so by the maximum modulus principle $|g| \le 1/r$ on $|z|\le r$. Fix $z$ and let $r \to 1$: $|g(z)| \le 1$, which gives both inequalities. If equality $|g|=1$ holds at an interior point, the maximum modulus principle forces $g$ to be a constant of modulus $1$.

blocks.title: Automorphisms of the disc
blocks.body: Every automorphism of $\mathbb{D}$ has the form $f(z) = e^{i\theta}\,\psi_\alpha(z)$ with $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and $|\alpha|<1$; conversely all such maps are automorphisms.

Let $f \in \operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{D})$ and $\alpha = f^{-1}(0)$. Then $g = f \circ \psi_\alpha$ is an automorphism with $g(0) = f(\alpha) = 0$. The Schwarz lemma applied to $g$ and to $g^{-1}$ gives $|g'(0)| \le 1$ and $|1/g'(0)| \le 1$, so $|g'(0)|=1$ and $g(z)=e^{i\theta}z$. Since $\psi_\alpha$ is its own inverse, $f = g \circ \psi_\alpha = e^{i\theta}\psi_\alpha$.

blocks.title: Riemann mapping theorem
blocks.body: Let $\Omega \subsetneq \mathbb{C}$ be a nonempty simply connected open set and $z_0 \in \Omega$. There is a unique conformal map $F: \Omega \to \mathbb{D}$ with $F(z_0) = 0$ and $F'(z_0) > 0$.

blocks.title: Proof (in three steps)
blocks.body:
Uniqueness: if $F_1, F_2$ both work, $F_2 \circ F_1^{-1}$ is an automorphism of $\mathbb{D}$ fixing $0$ with positive derivative there; by the Schwarz lemma argument above it is $z\mapsto e^{i\theta}z$ with $e^{i\theta}>0$, i.e. the identity.

Step 1 (move into the disc). Choose $\alpha \notin \Omega$. Then $z-\alpha$ never vanishes on the simply connected set $\Omega$, so it has a holomorphic square root $g$. The map $g$ is injective, and moreover $g(z_1) \neq -g(z_2)$ for all $z_1,z_2$ (squaring would give $z_1=z_2$ and then $g(z_1)=0$). By the open mapping theorem $g(\Omega)$ contains a disc $D(w_0,\rho)$ around $w_0 = g(z_0)$, so $g(\Omega)$ misses $D(-w_0,\rho)$. Hence $1/(g(z)+w_0)$ is injective and bounded by $1/\rho$; after scaling and translating we obtain an injective holomorphic map $\Omega \to \mathbb{D}$ sending $z_0$ to $0$.

Step 2 (extremal map). Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the family of injective holomorphic $f: \Omega\to\mathbb{D}$ with $f(z_0)=0$; it is nonempty, and $s = \sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}} |f'(z_0)|$ is positive (by the theorem on injective maps) and finite (Cauchy estimates). The family is uniformly bounded, so the Cauchy integral formula bounds the derivatives uniformly on each compact set; the family is therefore equicontinuous there, and Arzelà–Ascoli plus a diagonal argument (Montel's theorem) gives a sequence $f_n \in \mathcal{F}$ with $|f_n'(z_0)| \to s$ converging uniformly on compact sets to some holomorphic $f$. Then $|f'(z_0)| = s > 0$, so $f$ is not constant; by Hurwitz's theorem a locally uniform limit of injective holomorphic maps is injective or constant, so $f$ is injective. Finally $|f| \le 1$, and the maximum modulus principle gives $|f|<1$. So $f \in \mathcal{F}$.

Step 3 (the extremal map is onto). Suppose $f(\Omega)$ misses some $\alpha \in \mathbb{D}$. The map $\psi_\alpha \circ f$ never vanishes on $\Omega$, so it has a holomorphic square root $q$, with values in $\mathbb{D}$; $q$ is injective because $q^2 = \psi_\alpha\circ f$ is. Put $\beta = q(z_0)$ and $h = \psi_\beta \circ q$; then $h \in \mathcal{F}$. Writing $s(w) = w^2$, we have $f = \Phi \circ h$ with $\Phi = \psi_\alpha \circ s \circ \psi_\beta$. Now $\Phi$ maps $\mathbb{D}$ into $\mathbb{D}$, fixes $0$, and is not injective (because $s$ is not), so it is not a rotation and the Schwarz lemma gives $|\Phi'(0)|<1$. Then $|f'(z_0)| = |\Phi'(0)|\,|h'(z_0)| < |h'(z_0)|$, contradicting maximality. So $f$ is onto, and multiplying by a unimodular constant makes $f'(z_0)>0$.

blocks.title: The first quadrant
blocks.body: Find a conformal map from the open first quadrant $Q = \{x+iy: x>0,\ y>0\}$ onto $\mathbb{D}$, and find the point that goes to $0$.
blocks.solution:
In polar form, $Q$ is $0 < \arg z < \pi/2$, and $z \mapsto z^2$ doubles arguments, so it maps $Q$ bijectively onto the upper half-plane $0<\arg w<\pi$ (it is injective on $Q$ because $z^2 = z'^2$ forces $z' = \pm z$, and $-z \notin Q$). Then the Cayley map sends $\mathbb{H}$ onto $\mathbb{D}$. So
$$f(z) = \frac{i - z^2}{i + z^2}$$
works. It sends $z$ to $0$ exactly when $z^2 = i$, i.e. $z = e^{i\pi/4} = \tfrac{1+i}{\sqrt 2}$. As a spot check, $f(1+i) = \frac{i-2i}{i+2i} = -\frac13$, which lies in the disc.

blocks.title: A strip
blocks.body: Map the horizontal strip $S = \{0 < \operatorname{Im} z < \pi\}$ conformally onto $\mathbb{D}$.
blocks.solution: Write $z = x+iy$. Then $e^z = e^x e^{iy}$; as $x$ ranges over $\mathbb{R}$ the modulus $e^x$ covers $(0,\infty)$ once, and as $y$ ranges over $(0,\pi)$ the argument covers $(0,\pi)$ once. So $e^z$ maps $S$ bijectively onto $\mathbb{H}$, and $z \mapsto \dfrac{i-e^z}{i+e^z}$ maps $S$ onto $\mathbb{D}$. The point $z = i\pi/2$ goes to $e^{i\pi/2}=i$ and then to $0$.

blocks.title: How far can a disc map move the centre?
blocks.body: Let $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{D}$ be holomorphic. (a) If $f(\tfrac12)=0$, how large can $|f(0)|$ be? (b) If instead $f(0)=\tfrac12$, how large can $|f'(0)|$ be?
blocks.solution:
(a) Put $g = f \circ \psi_{1/2}$. Then $g(0) = f(\tfrac12) = 0$, so by the Schwarz lemma $|g(z)|\le|z|$. Since $\psi_{1/2}$ is its own inverse, $f = g\circ\psi_{1/2}$, so $f(0) = g(\psi_{1/2}(0)) = g(\tfrac12)$, so $|f(0)| \le \tfrac12$. Equality holds for $f = \psi_{1/2}$ itself, for which $f(0) = \tfrac12$.

(b) Now $k = \psi_{1/2}\circ f$ sends $0$ to $0$, so $|k'(0)| \le 1$. By the chain rule $k'(0) = \psi_{1/2}'(\tfrac12)\, f'(0)$, and from the derivative formula $\psi_\alpha'(\alpha) = \dfrac{|\alpha|^2-1}{(1-|\alpha|^2)^2} = -\dfrac{1}{1-|\alpha|^2}$, which is $-\tfrac43$ for $\alpha = \tfrac12$. Hence $|f'(0)| \le \tfrac34$, with equality for $f = \psi_{1/2}$, whose derivative at $0$ is $-\tfrac34$.

The general statement behind both parts is the Schwarz–Pick lemma: holomorphic self-maps of the disc never increase the hyperbolic distance, and in particular $|f'(z)| \le \dfrac{1-|f(z)|^2}{1-|z|^2}$.

blocks.body:
- The plane itself is excluded for a reason: a conformal map $\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{D}$ would be a bounded entire function, hence constant by Liouville's theorem.
- Simple connectivity is essential. An annulus $\{r<|z|<1\}$ is not conformally equivalent to the disc, and two annuli are equivalent only when their radius ratios agree.
- "Locally angle-preserving" is weaker than "conformal map" in the sense of this page: $e^z$ has nonvanishing derivative on all of $\mathbb{C}$ but is not injective.
- The theorem is purely existential and says nothing about boundary behaviour. Carathéodory's theorem adds that if $\partial\Omega$ is a Jordan curve, the map extends to a homeomorphism of the closures.

The proof uses [[holomorphic|Cauchy's theorem]] (for square roots on simply connected sets), the open mapping and maximum modulus principles, and the [[arzela-ascoli]] theorem in the form of Montel's theorem. Möbius maps are the complex-analytic face of the inversions in [[geo-transformations]], and "simply connected" is the condition of trivial [[fundamental-group]].

Since conformal maps carry harmonic functions to harmonic functions, they solve the Dirichlet problem for [[laplace-equation|Laplace's equation]] on simply connected regions. The disc with the metric invariant under $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{D})$ is the Poincaré model of hyperbolic geometry, a basic example in [[riemannian-geometry]]. The far-reaching generalisation is the uniformisation theorem: every simply connected Riemann surface is conformally the disc, the plane or the sphere.

1. Find a conformal map from the half-disc $\{|z|<1,\ \operatorname{Im} z>0\}$ onto the first quadrant. (Try a Möbius map sending $-1, 0, 1$ to $0, 1, \infty$.)
2. Show that a holomorphic $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{D}$ with two distinct fixed points is the identity.
3. Show that $z \mapsto \frac{az+b}{cz+d}$ with $a,b,c,d$ real and $ad-bc>0$ maps $\mathbb{H}$ onto itself.
4. Prove that $\Delta(u\circ f) = |f'|^2(\Delta u)\circ f$ for holomorphic $f$ using the Cauchy–Riemann equations.

entry.sum: The dual space $V^*$ of a vector space $V$ over $F$ is the space of linear functionals $V \to F$, and the quotient $V/U$ is the space of cosets $v+U$, obtained by declaring vectors of a subspace $U$ to be zero. For finite-dimensional $V$ both have predictable dimensions, and the transpose of a matrix turns out to be the dual map, which is why row rank equals column rank.
key: \dim V^* = \dim V,\qquad \dim U^0 = \dim V/U = \dim V - \dim U \qquad (\dim V < \infty)
V/\operatorname{null} T \;\cong\; \operatorname{range} T \qquad (\text{first isomorphism theorem})
\operatorname{null} T' = (\operatorname{range} T)^0,\qquad \mathcal{M}(T') = \mathcal{M}(T)^{\mathsf{T}} \ \ (\text{dual bases})
entry.why: Linear functionals are how one measures vectors: coordinates, evaluations of a polynomial at a point, integrals, and gradients of functions are all elements of a dual space, and quotients are the standard way to build new spaces by ignoring a subspace.

links.note: In infinite dimensions the dual space of a normed space is restricted to continuous functionals, and the Hahn–Banach and Riesz representation theorems describe it.
The cotangent space at a point of a manifold is the dual of the tangent space, and the differential $df$ of a function is a covector field.
In quantum mechanics a bra $\langle\phi|$ is the linear functional on state vectors defined by the inner product, and in relativity covectors carry lower indices.

blocks.body:
Asking for the second coordinate of a vector, evaluating a polynomial at $x=3$, and integrating a function over $[0,1]$ all do the same kind of thing: they take a vector and produce a number, linearly. Such maps are linear functionals, and collecting them gives a new vector space, the dual space. It is the natural home of "measurements" of vectors.

The second construction on this page goes the other way. Sometimes part of a space is irrelevant: we care about polynomials only through their value at $1$, or about vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ only up to adding multiples of a fixed direction. The quotient space formalises "work in $V$ but treat the subspace $U$ as zero". Duality and quotients turn out to be closely tied, and both rest on [[linear-maps|rank–nullity]].

blocks.title: Dual space
blocks.body:
Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$. A linear functional on $V$ is a linear map $\varphi: V \to F$. The dual space $V^* = \mathcal{L}(V, F)$ is the set of all linear functionals, a vector space under $(\varphi+\psi)(v) = \varphi(v)+\psi(v)$ and $(c\varphi)(v) = c\,\varphi(v)$.

On $F^n$, every functional has the form $\varphi(x) = a_1x_1+\dots+a_nx_n$, so functionals are row vectors and vectors are column vectors.

blocks.title: Dual basis
blocks.body: Let $v_1, \dots, v_n$ be a basis of $V$. Define $\varphi_j \in V^*$ by $\varphi_j(v_k) = 1$ if $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise. Then $\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n$ is a basis of $V^*$, called the dual basis, and every $\varphi \in V^*$ satisfies $\varphi = \sum_j \varphi(v_j)\,\varphi_j$. In particular $\dim V^* = \dim V$.

A linear map is determined by its values on a basis, and any values can be prescribed; so each $\varphi_j$ exists and is unique. Given $\varphi$, the functionals $\varphi$ and $\sum_j \varphi(v_j)\varphi_j$ agree on each $v_k$, hence everywhere; so the $\varphi_j$ span. If $\sum_j c_j\varphi_j = 0$, applying it to $v_k$ gives $c_k = 0$; so they are independent.

blocks.title: Computing dual bases
blocks.body:
Note that $\varphi_j(v)$ is just the $j$-th coordinate of $v$ in the basis $v_1,\dots,v_n$. In $F^n$ this gives a recipe: put the basis vectors as the columns of a matrix $B$; the coordinates of $x$ are $B^{-1}x$, so the dual basis functionals are the rows of $B^{-1}$.

For example take $v_1 = (1,1)$ and $v_2=(1,2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Then $B = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, $B^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}$, and $\varphi_1(x,y) = 2x-y$, $\varphi_2(x,y) = -x+y$. Check: $\varphi_1(1,1)=1$, $\varphi_1(1,2)=0$, $\varphi_2(1,1)=0$, $\varphi_2(1,2)=1$.

The same recipe shows a subtle point: $\varphi_1$ depends on the whole basis, not just on $v_1$. With the basis $(1,1),(0,1)$ instead, the first dual functional becomes $\varphi_1(x,y)=x$.

blocks.title: Annihilator
blocks.body:
For a subspace $U \subseteq V$, the annihilator is $U^0 = \{\varphi \in V^* : \varphi(u) = 0 \text{ for all } u \in U\}$, a subspace of $V^*$. If $V$ is finite-dimensional then $\dim U + \dim U^0 = \dim V$.

Meaning: a $k$-dimensional subspace of an $n$-dimensional space is cut out by exactly $n-k$ independent linear equations.

blocks.title: Proof of the dimension formula
blocks.body: Extend a basis $u_1,\dots,u_m$ of $U$ to a basis $u_1,\dots,u_m,v_{m+1},\dots,v_n$ of $V$, with dual basis $\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_n$. Call these basis vectors $w_1,\dots,w_n$ (so $w_i = u_i$ for $i\le m$). If $\varphi \in U^0$ then $\varphi = \sum_j \varphi(w_j)\,\varphi_j$ and the first $m$ coefficients vanish, so $\varphi \in \operatorname{span}(\varphi_{m+1},\dots,\varphi_n)$. Conversely each $\varphi_j$ with $j>m$ kills all $u_i$. So $U^0$ has basis $\varphi_{m+1},\dots,\varphi_n$ and dimension $n-m$.

blocks.title: The dual map and the transpose
blocks.body:
A linear map $T: V \to W$ induces a map the other way, $T': W^* \to V^*$, by $T'(\psi) = \psi \circ T$: to measure $v$, first push it to $W$ and measure there. One checks directly that $(ST)' = T'S'$.

If $V, W$ have bases with dual bases, and $A$ is the matrix of $T$, then the matrix of $T'$ is the transpose $A^{\mathsf{T}}$: the $(k,j)$ entry of the matrix of $T'$ is $T'(\psi_j)(v_k) = \psi_j(Tv_k) = A_{jk}$. This is the conceptual meaning of the transpose.

Two facts follow quickly. First, $\operatorname{null} T' = (\operatorname{range} T)^0$, because $\psi\circ T = 0$ means precisely that $\psi$ vanishes on the range of $T$. Second, by rank–nullity for $T'$ and the annihilator formula,
$$\dim\operatorname{range} T' = \dim W - \dim(\operatorname{range} T)^0 = \dim \operatorname{range} T.$$
Read through matrices, this says that $A^{\mathsf{T}}$ and $A$ have the same rank: row rank equals column rank.

blocks.title: The double dual
blocks.body:
There is no natural isomorphism $V \to V^*$: the dual basis construction depends on a choice of basis. But there is a natural map $\Lambda: V \to V^{**}$, given by $\Lambda(v)(\varphi) = \varphi(v)$, "evaluate at $v$". It is injective, since for $v\neq 0$ we can extend $v$ to a basis and the first dual functional gives $\varphi(v) = 1$. In finite dimensions $\dim V^{**} = \dim V$, so $\Lambda$ is an isomorphism, and it requires no choices.

In infinite dimensions the dual is genuinely bigger. For $V = \mathbb{Q}[x]$, a functional may take arbitrary values on $1, x, x^2, \dots$, so $V^*$ is the space of all sequences of rationals; it has uncountable dimension while $V$ has countable dimension. The coefficient functionals $p \mapsto (\text{coefficient of } x^n)$ are independent but do not span: $p \mapsto p(1)$ is not a finite combination of them.

blocks.title: Quotient space
blocks.body:
Let $U$ be a subspace of $V$. For $v \in V$, the coset $v + U = \{v+u : u \in U\}$. The quotient space $V/U$ is the set of cosets, with $(v+U)+(w+U) = (v+w)+U$ and $c(v+U) = cv+U$. The quotient map $\pi: V\to V/U$ is $\pi(v) = v+U$.

Two cosets are equal, $v+U = w+U$, exactly when $v-w \in U$; the operations are well defined because changing $v$ and $w$ by elements of $U$ changes $v+w$ and $cv$ by elements of $U$. Geometrically, $\mathbb{R}^3/\text{(a line)}$ is the set of lines parallel to it, which behaves like a plane.

blocks.title: First isomorphism theorem and dimension of a quotient
blocks.body: If $T: V \to W$ is linear, then $\tilde T(v + \operatorname{null}T) = Tv$ is a well-defined isomorphism $V/\operatorname{null}T \to \operatorname{range} T$. If $V$ is finite-dimensional, $\dim V/U = \dim V - \dim U$, and $(V/U)^* \cong U^0$ via $\varphi \mapsto \varphi\circ\pi$.

If $v + \operatorname{null}T = v' + \operatorname{null}T$ then $v-v' \in \operatorname{null}T$, so $Tv = Tv'$: $\tilde T$ is well defined, and it is clearly linear and onto $\operatorname{range}T$. If $\tilde T(v+\operatorname{null}T) = 0$ then $v\in\operatorname{null}T$, so the coset is zero: $\tilde T$ is injective.

The quotient map $\pi$ is linear and onto with null space $U$, so rank–nullity gives $\dim V = \dim U + \dim V/U$. Finally, $\varphi \mapsto \varphi\circ\pi$ is linear and injective (as $\pi$ is onto), its image lies in $U^0$, and every $\psi \in U^0$ arises because $\psi$ is constant on cosets and hence defines a functional on $V/U$.

blocks.title: Simpson's rule from a dual basis
blocks.body: On the space $\mathcal{P}_2$ of real polynomials of degree at most $2$, let $e_k(p) = p(k)$ for $k=0,1,2$. Show that $e_0,e_1,e_2$ is a basis of $\mathcal{P}_2^*$, find the basis of $\mathcal{P}_2$ it is dual to, and write the functional $I(p) = \int_0^2 p(x)\,dx$ in this basis.
blocks.solution:
The polynomials
$$L_0 = \tfrac12(x-1)(x-2),\qquad L_1 = -x(x-2),\qquad L_2 = \tfrac12 x(x-1)$$
satisfy $L_j(k) = 1$ if $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise, i.e. $e_k(L_j) = \delta_{jk}$. They are independent (apply $e_k$ to a vanishing combination), so they form a basis of the $3$-dimensional $\mathcal{P}_2$, and $e_0,e_1,e_2$ is exactly its dual basis. By the dual basis theorem, $I = I(L_0)e_0 + I(L_1)e_1 + I(L_2)e_2$. Integrating, $I(L_0) = \tfrac13$, $I(L_1) = \tfrac43$, $I(L_2) = \tfrac13$, so
$$\int_0^2 p(x)\,dx = \tfrac13\big(p(0) + 4p(1) + p(2)\big)\quad\text{for every } p\in\mathcal{P}_2.$$
This is Simpson's rule; the dual basis explains why three weights suffice and how to find them.

blocks.title: An annihilator and a quotient in $\mathbb{R}^4$
blocks.body: Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^4$ be spanned by $u_1 = (1,0,1,0)$ and $u_2 = (0,1,1,1)$. Find a basis of $U^0$, and use it to identify $\mathbb{R}^4/U$ with $\mathbb{R}^2$.
blocks.solution:
A functional $\varphi(x) = ax_1+bx_2+cx_3+dx_4$ kills $U$ iff $a + c = 0$ and $b+c+d=0$. Choosing $(c,d) = (1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ gives the basis
$$\varphi_1 = (-1,-1,1,0),\qquad \varphi_2 = (0,-1,0,1)$$
of $U^0$, which has dimension $4-2=2$ as predicted.

Now let $T:\mathbb{R}^4\to\mathbb{R}^2$, $T(x) = (\varphi_1(x),\varphi_2(x))$. Its null space contains $U$, and has dimension $4 - \operatorname{rank}T = 2$ since $\varphi_1,\varphi_2$ are independent; so $\operatorname{null}T = U$ and $T$ is onto. By the first isomorphism theorem $\mathbb{R}^4/U \cong \mathbb{R}^2$, with coset $x+U$ corresponding to $(\varphi_1(x),\varphi_2(x))$. For instance $(1,1,2,1) = u_1+u_2$ is in $U$, and indeed $T(1,1,2,1) = (0,0)$.

blocks.title: When does one functional depend on others?
blocks.body: Let $\varphi, \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_k$ be linear functionals on any vector space $V$ (not necessarily finite-dimensional). Prove that if every $v$ with $\varphi_1(v) = \dots = \varphi_k(v) = 0$ also satisfies $\varphi(v) = 0$, then $\varphi = c_1\varphi_1+\dots+c_k\varphi_k$ for some scalars $c_i$.
blocks.solution:
Define $T: V \to F^k$ by $T(v) = (\varphi_1(v),\dots,\varphi_k(v))$. The hypothesis says $\operatorname{null}T \subseteq \operatorname{null}\varphi$. So $\varphi$ is constant on cosets of $\operatorname{null}T$ and induces a functional $\bar\varphi$ on $V/\operatorname{null}T$. By the first isomorphism theorem $V/\operatorname{null}T \cong \operatorname{range}T \subseteq F^k$, so $\bar\varphi$ becomes a linear functional $\chi$ on the subspace $\operatorname{range}T$, with $\varphi = \chi\circ T$.

Extend $\chi$ to all of $F^k$ (extend a basis of $\operatorname{range}T$ to a basis of $F^k$ and send the new vectors to $0$). Every functional on $F^k$ has the form $y \mapsto c_1y_1+\dots+c_ky_k$, so $\varphi(v) = \chi(T v) = \sum_i c_i\varphi_i(v)$. The finite-dimensional space here is $F^k$, not $V$, which is why the result holds for every $V$. This lemma is the linear-algebra core of the method of Lagrange multipliers.

blocks.body:
- $V$ and $V^*$ have the same dimension in finite dimensions, but there is no basis-free isomorphism between them; on a real inner product space, $v\mapsto\langle\cdot,v\rangle$ is one ([[inner-products]]).
- The dual functional $\varphi_j$ is not determined by $v_j$ alone; it changes if the other basis vectors change.
- In infinite dimensions the "dual basis" does not span $V^*$ and $V \to V^{**}$ is not onto.
- A coset $v+U$ with $v\notin U$ is not a subspace (it does not contain $0$); it is the element of $V/U$, and the zero element of $V/U$ is the coset $U$ itself.
- The dual map goes backwards, $T': W^*\to V^*$, and $(ST)' = T'S'$ reverses order, just as $(AB)^{\mathsf{T}} = B^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}$.

Dual spaces are the starting point of multilinear algebra: bilinear forms are elements of $(V\otimes V)^*$ and tensors of type $(p,q)$ mix copies of $V$ and $V^*$ ([[tensor-products]]). In analysis one keeps only continuous functionals, and the [[hahn-banach]] theorem guarantees that there are enough of them; on a Hilbert space they are all inner products with a fixed vector ([[hilbert-spaces]]). The cotangent vectors and the differential forms of [[differential-forms]] are dual objects, and the quotient construction is the linear version of the quotient groups of [[group-homomorphisms]] and quotient rings of [[rings]].

2. Find weights $a,b$ such that $\int_{-1}^1 p(x)\,dx = a\,p(-1/\sqrt3) + b\,p(1/\sqrt3)$ for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most $1$, and check that the formula still holds for degree $3$.

entry.sum: The tensor product $V\otimes W$ is the vector space that turns bilinear maps out of $V\times W$ into linear maps; if $e_i$ and $f_j$ are bases, the $e_i\otimes f_j$ form a basis, so $\dim(V\otimes W) = \dim V\cdot\dim W$. The exterior power $\Lambda^k V$ does the same for alternating multilinear maps, with $v\wedge w = -w\wedge v$, and its top degree $\Lambda^n V$ is one-dimensional with the determinant as its scaling factor.
key: \operatorname{Bil}(V\times W, U) \;\cong\; \mathcal{L}(V\otimes W, U),\qquad \dim (V\otimes W) = \dim V \cdot \dim W
\dim \Lambda^k V = \binom{n}{k},\qquad v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n = \det(A)\; e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_n
V^*\otimes W \;\cong\; \mathcal{L}(V,W) \quad (\text{finite dimensions})
entry.why: Tensors are the language for anything multilinear: bilinear forms, the metric and curvature of a space, stress in a material, and the joint state of two quantum systems, while the exterior algebra underlies determinants, oriented volume and differential forms.

links.note: A Riemannian metric is a symmetric tensor field of type $(0,2)$, and differential $k$-forms are sections of the $k$-th exterior power of the cotangent bundle.
The state space of $n$ qubits is the tensor product of $n$ copies of $\mathbb{C}^2$, and an entangled state is exactly a tensor that is not a pure tensor.
Tensor products, symmetric powers and exterior powers of representations are the basic ways of building new representations from old ones.

blocks.body:
Many basic operations are linear in each of two inputs separately: the dot product, the cross product, matrix multiplication, the determinant of a $2\times2$ matrix as a function of its columns. Such maps are bilinear, and they are not linear maps on the product $V\times W$: doubling both inputs quadruples the output. The tensor product is a cleverly built space $V\otimes W$ in which bilinear maps become ordinary linear maps, so that all the tools of linear algebra apply to them.

The second half of the page specialises to maps that change sign when two inputs are swapped. These are governed by the exterior algebra, and the top exterior power gives the cleanest possible account of the [[determinants|determinant]]. Familiarity with [[dual-spaces]] is assumed.

blocks.title: Bilinear maps
blocks.body:
A map $\beta: V\times W \to U$ is bilinear if $\beta(v, w)$ is linear in $v$ for each fixed $w$, and linear in $w$ for each fixed $v$. Examples: $\beta(x,y) = x\cdot y$ on $\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n$; $\beta(x,y) = x\times y$ on $\mathbb{R}^3\times\mathbb{R}^3$; $\beta(\varphi, w) = \varphi(w)$ on $V^*\times V$; and $\beta(p,q) = p(x)q(y)$, sending two polynomials in one variable to a polynomial in two variables.

If $e_1,\dots,e_m$ and $f_1,\dots,f_n$ are bases, bilinearity gives
$$\beta\Big(\sum_i a_ie_i,\ \sum_j b_jf_j\Big) = \sum_{i,j} a_ib_j\,\beta(e_i,f_j),$$
so $\beta$ is determined by the $mn$ vectors $\beta(e_i,f_j)$, and these can be chosen freely. That count, $mn$ rather than $m+n$, is the dimension of the space we are about to build.

blocks.title: Tensor product
blocks.body:
A tensor product of $V$ and $W$ is a vector space $V\otimes W$ with a bilinear map $V\times W\to V\otimes W$, $(v,w)\mapsto v\otimes w$, that is universal: for every bilinear $\beta: V\times W\to U$ there is a unique linear $\tilde\beta: V\otimes W\to U$ with $\tilde\beta(v\otimes w) = \beta(v,w)$.

Elements of the form $v\otimes w$ are pure (or simple) tensors; a general element of $V\otimes W$ is a sum of them.

blocks.title: Existence, uniqueness and a basis
blocks.body: A tensor product exists and is unique up to a unique isomorphism compatible with $\otimes$. If $e_1,\dots,e_m$ is a basis of $V$ and $f_1,\dots,f_n$ a basis of $W$, then the $mn$ vectors $e_i\otimes f_j$ form a basis of $V\otimes W$.

Existence (for finite-dimensional $V, W$; in general one takes the vector space with a basis indexed by all pairs $(v,w)$ and divides by the subspace spanned by the bilinearity relations): let $T$ be a vector space with a basis of $mn$ symbols $t_{ij}$, and define $v\otimes w = \sum_{i,j} a_ib_j\,t_{ij}$ where $a_i, b_j$ are the coordinates of $v, w$. This is bilinear and $e_i\otimes f_j = t_{ij}$. Given bilinear $\beta$, define $\tilde\beta$ on the basis by $\tilde\beta(t_{ij}) = \beta(e_i,f_j)$; by the expansion above, $\tilde\beta(v\otimes w) = \beta(v,w)$. It is unique because the $t_{ij}$ are pure tensors spanning $T$, so the values of $\tilde\beta$ are forced. Thus $T$ is a tensor product with basis $e_i\otimes f_j$.

Uniqueness: if $(T_1,\otimes_1)$ and $(T_2,\otimes_2)$ are both universal, applying the universal property of each to the other's bilinear map gives linear maps $T_1\to T_2$ and $T_2\to T_1$ preserving pure tensors. Their composites fix every pure tensor of $T_1$ (resp. $T_2$), and by the uniqueness clause the only such linear map is the identity. So both maps are inverse isomorphisms.

blocks.title: Pure tensors, rank and matrices
blocks.body:
Write a tensor as $\tau = \sum_{i,j} c_{ij}\, e_i\otimes f_j$ and record its coefficients as an $m\times n$ matrix $C$. A pure tensor $v\otimes w$ has $c_{ij} = a_ib_j$, i.e. $C = ab^{\mathsf{T}}$, a matrix of rank at most $1$. Conversely every rank-one matrix is of this form. So most tensors are not pure: $e_1\otimes f_1 + e_2\otimes f_2$ has coefficient matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ of rank $2$. The least number of pure tensors needed to write $\tau$ equals $\operatorname{rank} C$.

This is an instance of the identification $V^*\otimes W\cong\mathcal{L}(V,W)$ in finite dimensions, sending $\varphi\otimes w$ to the map $v\mapsto\varphi(v)\,w$. Pure tensors become rank-one maps, and every linear map is a sum of $\operatorname{rank}$ many of them. Similarly $V^*\otimes V^*$ is the space of bilinear forms on $V$, and a tensor of type $(p,q)$ is an element of $V^{\otimes p}\otimes (V^*)^{\otimes q}$. In physics, writing such a tensor in coordinates gives the familiar arrays with upper and lower indices.

Linear maps tensor too: $A: V\to V'$ and $B:W\to W'$ give $A\otimes B$ with $(A\otimes B)(v\otimes w) = Av\otimes Bw$. In the basis $e_i\otimes f_j$ (ordered lexicographically) its matrix is the Kronecker product, the block matrix $(a_{ij}B)$. From $(A\otimes B)(C\otimes D) = AC\otimes BD$ one gets, for $A$ of size $m\times m$ and $B$ of size $n\times n$,
$$\operatorname{tr}(A\otimes B) = \operatorname{tr}A\cdot\operatorname{tr}B,\qquad \det(A\otimes B) = (\det A)^n(\det B)^m.$$

blocks.title: Exterior power
blocks.body:
A multilinear map $\alpha: V^k\to U$ is alternating if $\alpha(v_1,\dots,v_k) = 0$ whenever two of the $v_i$ are equal. The $k$-th exterior power $\Lambda^kV$ is a vector space with an alternating multilinear map $(v_1,\dots,v_k)\mapsto v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_k$ that is universal for alternating multilinear maps out of $V^k$. Concretely, $\Lambda^kV = V^{\otimes k}/I_k$, where $I_k$ is spanned by all pure tensors with two equal factors (a [[dual-spaces|quotient space]]).

Expanding $(v+w)\wedge(v+w) = 0$ shows $v\wedge w = -w\wedge v$: swapping two factors changes the sign.

blocks.title: Basis of the exterior power
blocks.body: If $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is a basis of $V$, then the vectors $e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_k}$ with $i_1<i_2<\dots<i_k$ form a basis of $\Lambda^kV$. Hence $\dim\Lambda^kV = \binom nk$, $\Lambda^kV = 0$ for $k>n$, and the exterior algebra $\Lambda V = \bigoplus_{k=0}^n\Lambda^kV$ has dimension $2^n$.

blocks.title: Proof sketch
blocks.body: Spanning: expand each $v_j$ in the basis; every resulting wedge of basis vectors with a repeat is $0$, and the others can be sorted into increasing order at the cost of a sign. Independence: for each increasing index set $J = (j_1<\dots<j_k)$, the function $\alpha_J(v_1,\dots,v_k) = \det$ of the $k\times k$ matrix formed by rows $j_1,\dots,j_k$ of the coordinate columns of the $v$'s is alternating and multilinear, so it induces a linear functional on $\Lambda^kV$. It takes the value $1$ on $e_J$ and $0$ on every other $e_{J'}$, so a vanishing combination of the $e_J$ has all coefficients zero.

blocks.title: Top degree and the determinant
blocks.body:
Let $\dim V = n$ and let $v_j = \sum_i a_{ij}e_i$, so $A = (a_{ij})$ has the coordinates of $v_j$ as its $j$-th column. Then
$$v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n = \det(A)\;e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_n.$$
Consequently $v_1,\dots,v_k$ are linearly independent if and only if $v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_k\neq 0$, and for linear maps $S,T: V\to V$, $\det(ST) = \det S\det T$.

Expanding by multilinearity, $v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n = \sum a_{i_11}\cdots a_{i_nn}\,e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_n}$. Terms with a repeated index vanish, so only $i = \sigma$ a permutation survives, and sorting $e_{\sigma(1)}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{\sigma(n)}$ takes as many swaps as the parity of $\sigma$. The coefficient is $\sum_\sigma \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_j a_{\sigma(j)j} = \det A$, the Leibniz formula.

If the $v_i$ are dependent, one is a combination of the others and the wedge expands into terms with repeated factors, so it is $0$. If they are independent, extend to a basis $v_1,\dots,v_n$; the wedge of the whole basis is a nonzero multiple of $e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_n$ (its matrix is invertible), so the partial wedge cannot be $0$.

Finally a linear map $T$ induces $\Lambda^nT$ on the one-dimensional space $\Lambda^nV$ by $v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n\mapsto Tv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge Tv_n$; by the formula it is multiplication by $\det T$. Since $\Lambda^n(ST) = \Lambda^nS\circ\Lambda^nT$, the determinants multiply.

blocks.title: Wedges in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the cross product
blocks.body: Compute $a\wedge b$ for $a = a_1e_1+a_2e_2+a_3e_3$ and $b = b_1e_1+b_2e_2+b_3e_3$, and compare with $a\times b$.
blocks.solution:
Expand and use $e_i\wedge e_i = 0$ and $e_j\wedge e_i = -e_i\wedge e_j$:
$$a\wedge b = (a_1b_2-a_2b_1)\,e_1\wedge e_2 + (a_1b_3-a_3b_1)\,e_1\wedge e_3 + (a_2b_3-a_3b_2)\,e_2\wedge e_3.$$
The three coefficients are, up to order and one sign, the components of $a\times b = (a_2b_3-a_3b_2,\ a_3b_1-a_1b_3,\ a_1b_2-a_2b_1)$. The wedge is the more honest object: it lives in $\Lambda^2\mathbb{R}^3$, it exists in every dimension, and its coefficients are the signed areas of the projections of the parallelogram spanned by $a$ and $b$ onto the coordinate planes. Only in dimension $3$ does $\Lambda^2$ have the same dimension as $V$, which is why the cross product is special to $\mathbb{R}^3$.

blocks.title: Kronecker products
blocks.body: Let $A = \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Write down $A\otimes B$ and verify the trace and determinant formulas.
blocks.solution:
The Kronecker product is the block matrix
$$A\otimes B = \begin{pmatrix}1\cdot B & 2\cdot B\\ 0\cdot B & 3\cdot B\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2&1&4&2\\1&1&2&2\\0&0&6&3\\0&0&3&3\end{pmatrix}.$$
Its trace is $2+1+6+3 = 12 = \operatorname{tr}A\cdot\operatorname{tr}B = 4\cdot 3$. It is block upper triangular, so its determinant is $\det(B)\det(3B) = 1\cdot 9 = 9$, matching $(\det A)^2(\det B)^2 = 3^2\cdot1^2$. Conceptually, if $Ax = \lambda x$ and $By=\mu y$ then $(A\otimes B)(x\otimes y) = \lambda\mu\,(x\otimes y)$: the eigenvalues of $A\otimes B$ are the products $\lambda_i\mu_j$, here $1\cdot\mu_j$ and $3\cdot\mu_j$.

blocks.title: Which 2-vectors are pure? The Plücker relation
blocks.body: Show that $\omega\in\Lambda^2\mathbb{R}^4$ is a pure wedge $v\wedge w$ if and only if $\omega\wedge\omega=0$. Writing $\omega = \sum_{i<j}p_{ij}\,e_i\wedge e_j$, express this as one equation in the $p_{ij}$, and test it on $v = (1,2,0,1)$, $w = (0,1,1,3)$ and on $e_1\wedge e_2+e_3\wedge e_4$.
blocks.solution:
If $\omega = v\wedge w$ then $\omega\wedge\omega = v\wedge w\wedge v\wedge w = 0$ because $v$ is repeated. Expanding $\omega\wedge\omega$ in general, only products of $e_i\wedge e_j$ and $e_k\wedge e_l$ with $\{i,j,k,l\} = \{1,2,3,4\}$ survive, and collecting signs gives
$$\omega\wedge\omega = 2\,(p_{12}p_{34} - p_{13}p_{24} + p_{14}p_{23})\; e_1\wedge e_2\wedge e_3\wedge e_4.$$
For the converse, suppose $\omega\neq0$ and the relation holds; after renumbering the basis we may assume $p_{12}\neq0$. Put
$$v = e_1 - \frac{p_{23}}{p_{12}}e_3 - \frac{p_{24}}{p_{12}}e_4,\qquad w = p_{12}e_2+p_{13}e_3+p_{14}e_4.$$
Expanding $v\wedge w$ gives the coefficients $p_{12},p_{13},p_{14},p_{23},p_{24}$ directly, and the coefficient of $e_3\wedge e_4$ comes out as $(p_{13}p_{24}-p_{14}p_{23})/p_{12}$, which equals $p_{34}$ precisely because of the relation. So $\omega = v\wedge w$. The condition $p_{12}p_{34} - p_{13}p_{24} + p_{14}p_{23} = 0$ is the Plücker relation.

For $v = (1,2,0,1)$, $w = (0,1,1,3)$ we have $p_{ij} = v_iw_j-v_jw_i$: $p_{12}=1$, $p_{13}=1$, $p_{14}=3$, $p_{23}=2$, $p_{24}=5$, $p_{34}=-1$, and indeed $1\cdot(-1) - 1\cdot5 + 3\cdot2 = 0$. For $\omega = e_1\wedge e_2+e_3\wedge e_4$, $p_{12}p_{34} = 1$ and the other products vanish, so $\omega\wedge\omega = 2\,e_1\wedge e_2\wedge e_3\wedge e_4\neq0$: this $2$-vector is not the wedge of any two vectors. The $p_{ij}$ of pure wedges are the Plücker coordinates of the plane spanned by $v,w$.

blocks.body:
- Not every element of $V\otimes W$ is of the form $v\otimes w$; most are sums of several pure tensors.
- $v\otimes w$ and $w\otimes v$ are different elements of $V\otimes V$ in general, while $v\wedge w = -w\wedge v$.
- $\dim(V\otimes W)$ is the product of dimensions; the direct sum $V\oplus W$ has the sum.
- Pure tensors are not unique representations: $(2v)\otimes w = v\otimes(2w)$.
- In characteristic $2$, "alternating" ($\alpha(v,v)=0$) is stronger than "antisymmetric" ($\alpha(v,w) = -\alpha(w,v)$); the definition via repeated factors is the right one in general.
- Over rings rather than fields, tensor products can collapse: as abelian groups, $\mathbb{Z}/2\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Z}/3 = 0$, because $$x\otimes y = 3x\otimes y - 2x\otimes y = x\otimes 3y - 2x\otimes y = 0$$.

Exterior powers of the cotangent space are where [[differential-forms]] live, and the wedge product of forms is the wedge of this page applied pointwise. A metric is a symmetric tensor in $V^*\otimes V^*$, and curvature in [[riemannian-geometry]] is a tensor of type $(1,3)$. The same universal-property construction works for [[modules]] over any commutative ring, and tensor products of [[group-representations]] give new representations. The determinant identities on this page recover the main results of [[determinants]] without cofactor expansions.

2. Prove that $\operatorname{tr}: V^*\otimes V\to F$ defined by $\varphi\otimes v\mapsto\varphi(v)$ agrees with the matrix trace under $V^*\otimes V\cong\mathcal{L}(V,V)$.

entry.sum: When $Ax=b$ has no solution, the least-squares solution $\hat x$ minimises $\|Ax-b\|$; geometrically $A\hat x$ is the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto the column space of $A$, so the error $b-A\hat x$ is perpendicular to every column. This gives the normal equations $A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat x = A^{\mathsf{T}}b$, and in practice one solves them stably through a QR factorisation $A=QR$.
key: \|b - A\hat x\| = \min_x \|b-Ax\| \iff A^{\mathsf{T}}(b - A\hat x) = 0 \iff A^{\mathsf{T}}A\,\hat x = A^{\mathsf{T}}b
P = A(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf{T}},\qquad P^2 = P = P^{\mathsf{T}}\qquad(\text{independent columns})
A = QR,\ Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q = I,\ R \text{ upper triangular} \;\Longrightarrow\; R\hat x = Q^{\mathsf{T}}b
entry.why: Least squares is how a model is fitted to more measurements than unknowns, from a straight line through data points to GPS positioning and the calibration of instruments, and the projection picture behind it reappears in Fourier series and statistics.

links.note: Minimising $\|Ax-b\|^2$ is the model convex quadratic problem, and Gauss–Newton methods for nonlinear fitting solve a linear least-squares problem at every step.
The projection theorem in Hilbert spaces says the closest point of a closed subspace is the orthogonal projection, which is the infinite-dimensional form of the normal equations.
The partial sums of a Fourier series are the least-squares best approximations by trigonometric polynomials, because they are orthogonal projections in $L^2$.

refs: Boyd & Vandenberghe, Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra

blocks.body:
Suppose you measure a quantity at four times and expect it to grow linearly. Four points almost never lie on one line, so the system "line passes through all four points" has no solution. What should you do? The method of least squares, used by Legendre and Gauss around 1800 to fit planetary orbits, says: choose the line that makes the sum of squared errors as small as possible.

The answer has a clean geometric meaning. The best approximation to $b$ by vectors of the form $Ax$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $b$ to the column space of $A$. This page develops that picture using [[inner-products]] and [[linear-maps]], derives the normal equations, and explains why numerical software solves them via the QR factorisation instead.

blocks.title: Projecting onto a line
blocks.body:
Start with one direction $a\neq0$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and a vector $b$. The closest multiple $\hat c\,a$ to $b$ is the one for which the error $b-\hat c a$ is perpendicular to $a$: $a\cdot(b-\hat ca) = 0$, so
$$\hat c = \frac{a\cdot b}{a\cdot a},\qquad p = \frac{a\cdot b}{a\cdot a}\,a.$$
For $a = (1,1,1)$ and $b = (1,2,6)$ this gives $\hat c = 9/3 = 3$, $p = (3,3,3)$ and error $b-p = (-2,-1,3)$, which is perpendicular to $a$. Notice that $\hat c=3$ is the mean of the entries of $b$: the mean is the least-squares fit of a constant.

Why perpendicular? For any other multiple $ca$, Pythagoras gives $\|b-ca\|^2 = \|b-p\|^2 + (c-\hat c)^2\|a\|^2 \ge \|b-p\|^2$. The same argument works for any subspace.

blocks.title: Best approximation by orthogonal projection
blocks.body:
Let $W$ be a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}^m$. There is a unique $p\in W$ with $b-p\perp W$ (the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto $W$), and for every $w\in W$ with $w\neq p$,
$$\|b-w\| > \|b-p\|.$$
If $W$ is the column space of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$, then $p = A\hat x$ exactly when $\hat x$ solves the normal equations $A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat x = A^{\mathsf{T}}b$. These always have a solution, and the solution is unique if and only if the columns of $A$ are linearly independent.

Minimality: if $b-p\perp W$ and $w\in W$, then $p-w\in W$ is perpendicular to $b-p$, so $\|b-w\|^2 = \|b-p\|^2+\|p-w\|^2$, which exceeds $\|b-p\|^2$ unless $w=p$. This also shows $p$ is unique, since any other candidate would have to be strictly closer and strictly farther at once.

Normal equations: $b - Ax\perp W$ means $b-Ax$ is perpendicular to each column of $A$, i.e. $A^{\mathsf{T}}(b-Ax) = 0$.

Existence: every subspace $W$ is the column space of some matrix $A$ (take a basis of $W$ as columns), so it suffices to treat that case. $A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ and $A$ have the same null space, because $A^{\mathsf{T}}Ax = 0$ implies $\|Ax\|^2 = x^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}Ax = 0$. By rank–nullity they have the same rank, so the column space of $A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ (contained in that of $A^{\mathsf{T}}$) equals the column space of $A^{\mathsf{T}}$, which contains $A^{\mathsf{T}}b$. Hence the normal equations are solvable, and any solution gives a projection $p = A\hat x$. The solution is unique iff $\operatorname{null}(A^{\mathsf{T}}A) = \operatorname{null}A = 0$, i.e. iff the columns are independent.

blocks.title: The projection matrix
blocks.body:
When the columns of $A$ are independent, $A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ is invertible and
$$\hat x = (A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf{T}}b,\qquad p = Pb,\quad P = A(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf{T}}.$$
The matrix $P$ depends only on the subspace, not on the choice of basis columns. It is symmetric, $P^{\mathsf{T}} = P$, and idempotent, $P^2 = P$: projecting twice changes nothing. Conversely every symmetric idempotent matrix is the orthogonal projection onto its column space. The complementary matrix $I-P$ projects onto the orthogonal complement, and $b = Pb + (I-P)b$ splits $b$ into "explained" and "error" parts. For a single column $a$, $P = aa^{\mathsf{T}}/(a^{\mathsf{T}}a)$, recovering the line case.

blocks.title: Fitting a line to four points
blocks.body: Find the least-squares line $y = C + Dt$ through the made-up data points $(0,1), (1,3), (2,4), (3,4)$, and check that the error vector is perpendicular to the columns.
blocks.solution:
The system $C + Dt_i = y_i$ is $Ax = b$ with
$$A = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix},\quad x = \begin{pmatrix}C\\D\end{pmatrix},\quad b = \begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\4\\4\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then $A^{\mathsf{T}}A = \begin{pmatrix}4&6\\6&14\end{pmatrix}$ and $A^{\mathsf{T}}b = \begin{pmatrix}12\\23\end{pmatrix}$. Solving $4C+6D = 12$, $6C+14D = 23$ gives $D = 1$, $C = 3/2$. The best line is $y = \tfrac32 + t$.

The fitted values are $\tfrac32,\tfrac52,\tfrac72,\tfrac92$, and the error $e = b - A\hat x = (-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac12,-\tfrac12)$. Its dot product with $(1,1,1,1)$ is $0$ (errors sum to zero) and with $(0,1,2,3)$ is $\tfrac12+1-\tfrac32 = 0$. The minimum sum of squared errors is $\|e\|^2 = 1$. Note that what is minimised is the sum of squared vertical distances, not perpendicular distances to the line.

blocks.title: Gram–Schmidt and the QR factorisation
blocks.body:
Projection is easy when the basis of $W$ is orthonormal: if $q_1,\dots,q_n$ are orthonormal, then $p = \sum_j (q_j\cdot b)\,q_j$, with no system to solve. Gram–Schmidt produces such a basis from independent columns $a_1,\dots,a_n$: subtract from $a_k$ its projections onto $q_1,\dots,q_{k-1}$ and normalise. Since each $a_k$ is a combination of $q_1,\dots,q_k$, this is a factorisation
$$A = QR,$$
where $Q$ is $m\times n$ with orthonormal columns ($Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q = I$) and $R$ is $n\times n$ upper triangular with positive diagonal; $r_{jk} = q_j\cdot a_k$.

Substituting into the normal equations gives $R^{\mathsf{T}}Q^{\mathsf{T}}QR\hat x = R^{\mathsf{T}}Q^{\mathsf{T}}b$, and since $R^{\mathsf{T}}$ is invertible,
$$R\hat x = Q^{\mathsf{T}}b,$$
a triangular system solved by back-substitution. The projection matrix becomes simply $P = QQ^{\mathsf{T}}$.

The reason to prefer this numerically: the condition number of $A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ is the square of that of $A$. If $A$ has condition number $10^8$, forming $A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ in double precision (about 16 digits) can destroy every significant digit, while QR works with $A$ itself. Library routines compute $Q$ and $R$ by Householder reflections, which are more stable than classical Gram–Schmidt; the result is the same factorisation up to the signs of the columns of $Q$ and the rows of $R$.

blocks.title: The same fit via QR
blocks.body: Compute the QR factorisation of the matrix $A$ from the line-fitting example and use it to recover $C$ and $D$.
blocks.solution:
First column: $a_1 = (1,1,1,1)$ has length $2$, so $q_1 = \tfrac12(1,1,1,1)$ and $r_{11} = 2$.

Second column: $a_2 = (0,1,2,3)$, $r_{12} = q_1\cdot a_2 = 3$, and $a_2 - 3q_1 = (-\tfrac32,-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac32)$, of length $\sqrt5$. So $r_{22} = \sqrt5$ and $q_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(-\tfrac32,-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac32)$. Thus
$$R = \begin{pmatrix}2&3\\0&\sqrt5\end{pmatrix}.$$
Next $Q^{\mathsf{T}}b = (q_1\cdot b,\ q_2\cdot b) = (6,\ \sqrt5)$, because $q_2\cdot b = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(-\tfrac32-\tfrac32+2+6) = \tfrac{5}{\sqrt5}$. Back-substitution: $\sqrt5\,D = \sqrt5$ gives $D=1$, then $2C+3 = 6$ gives $C = \tfrac32$, as before.

blocks.title: Least squares for functions
blocks.body: Find real numbers $a, b$ minimising $\displaystyle\int_0^1 (x^2 - a - bx)^2\,dx$, and find the minimum value.
blocks.solution:
Work in the space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle = \int_0^1 fg\,dx$. We want the orthogonal projection of $x^2$ onto $W = \operatorname{span}\{1,x\}$. The normal equations say the error $x^2-a-bx$ is orthogonal to $1$ and to $x$:
$$\int_0^1(x^2-a-bx)\,dx = \tfrac13 - a - \tfrac b2 = 0,\qquad \int_0^1(x^2-a-bx)\,x\,dx = \tfrac14-\tfrac a2-\tfrac b3 = 0.$$
Solving, $b = 1$ and $a = -\tfrac16$. The best line is $x - \tfrac16$, and the error is $e(x) = x^2 - x + \tfrac16$. Since $e\perp W$, the minimum is
$$\int_0^1 e(x)^2\,dx = \int_0^1 e(x)\,x^2\,dx = \tfrac15 - \tfrac14 + \tfrac1{18} = \tfrac1{180}.$$
The same reasoning in infinite dimensions is the projection theorem in [[hilbert-spaces]]; the error polynomial $x^2-x+\frac16$ is, up to a constant, the second Legendre polynomial shifted to $[0,1]$.

blocks.title: Rank-deficient problems and the pseudoinverse
blocks.body: If the columns of $A$ are dependent, the projection $p$ is still unique but $\hat x$ is not: any vector of $\operatorname{null}A$ can be added. The standard choice is the solution of smallest norm, which is the unique solution lying in the row space of $A$. It is $\hat x = A^+b$, where $A^+$ is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse, computed most reliably from the [[svd]]: if $A = U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}$ then $A^+ = V\Sigma^+U^{\mathsf{T}}$, with $\Sigma^+$ inverting the nonzero singular values. For full column rank, $A^+ = (A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf{T}}$.

- The least-squares solution does not solve $Ax=b$; it solves $A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat x = A^{\mathsf{T}}b$. If $b$ happens to lie in the column space, the two agree.
- $Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q = I$ but $QQ^{\mathsf{T}}\neq I$ when $Q$ is not square; $QQ^{\mathsf{T}}$ is the projection $P$.
- Projection matrices are not invertible (unless $P = I$): information perpendicular to $W$ is lost.
- Forming $A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ squares the condition number; use QR or the SVD for ill-conditioned problems.
- Regressing $y$ on $t$ and regressing $t$ on $y$ give different lines, because they minimise different (vertical versus horizontal) errors.
- Squared errors make the fit sensitive to outliers; a single wild data point can tilt the line considerably.

In statistics, least squares with a probability model for the errors becomes [[linear-regression]], where $\hat x$ is the vector of fitted coefficients and $\|e\|^2$ the residual sum of squares. The minimum-norm solution and the best low-rank approximations both come from the [[svd]]. Minimising $\|Ax-b\|^2$ is the simplest problem in [[convex-optimisation]], and it can also be attacked iteratively by [[gradient-descent]], which is how very large fits are done. The best-approximation property of orthogonal projection explains why [[fourier-series]] partial sums are optimal in the mean-square sense, and polynomial least-squares fitting is a close relative of the [[interpolation-quadrature|interpolation]] methods of numerical analysis.

1. Find the least-squares solution of $x_1 + x_2 = 1$, $x_1 - x_2 = 1$, $x_1 = 3$.
2. Show that if $P$ is the projection onto $W$, then $I-P$ is the projection onto $W^\perp$, and $(I-P)P = 0$.
3. Fit a parabola $y = C+Dt+Et^2$ to the points $(-1,2),(0,0),(1,1),(2,5)$ by the normal equations.
4. Show that if $A$ has orthonormal columns then the least-squares solution is $\hat x = A^{\mathsf{T}}b$, and explain the result geometrically.

entry.sum: A group is solvable if it can be built from abelian groups in finitely many layers: its derived series $G \trianglerighteq G' \trianglerighteq G'' \trianglerighteq \cdots$ of commutator subgroups reaches the trivial group. Nilpotent groups are the stronger case in which repeatedly commutating with the whole group, $\gamma_{i+1} = [\gamma_i, G]$, reaches the identity; every finite $p$-group is nilpotent, and $S_n$ is solvable only for $n\le 4$.
key: G^{(0)} = G,\quad G^{(i+1)} = [G^{(i)}, G^{(i)}];\qquad G \text{ solvable} \iff G^{(k)} = 1 \text{ for some } k
N \trianglelefteq G:\quad G \text{ solvable} \iff N \text{ and } G/N \text{ solvable}
\text{abelian} \Rightarrow \text{nilpotent} \Rightarrow \text{solvable},\qquad |G| = p^n \Rightarrow G \text{ nilpotent}
entry.why: Solvability is exactly the group-theoretic condition in Galois's criterion for solving a polynomial equation by radicals, and since $A_5$ is not solvable, the general quintic has no formula in radicals.

links.note: Burnside's theorem that groups of order $p^aq^b$ are solvable was first proved with character theory, and solvable and nilpotent Lie algebras are the subject of Lie's and Engel's theorems.
A Galois extension of number fields has solvable Galois group exactly when it is a tower of abelian extensions, and abelian extensions are what class field theory describes.

refs: Rotman, An Introduction to the Theory of Groups

blocks.body:
Abelian groups are well understood; non-abelian groups can be wild. A natural strategy for understanding a group is to break it into layers using normal subgroups and quotients, as in [[group-homomorphisms]]. Solvable groups are those that can be broken into finitely many abelian layers. The name comes from Galois: a polynomial equation can be solved by a formula involving $+,-,\times,\div$ and $n$-th roots exactly when its Galois group is solvable.

This page defines solvable and nilpotent groups through commutators, proves that solvability passes to subgroups, quotients and extensions, shows that $p$-groups are nilpotent using the class equation from [[group-actions]], and works through the symmetric and dihedral groups.

blocks.title: Commutators and the derived subgroup
blocks.body:
The commutator of $x, y\in G$ is $[x,y] = x^{-1}y^{-1}xy$, so that $xy = yx[x,y]$. For subgroups $H, K$, $[H,K]$ is the subgroup generated by all $[h,k]$. The derived (commutator) subgroup is $G' = [G,G]$, and the derived series is
$$G^{(0)} = G,\qquad G^{(i+1)} = \big(G^{(i)}\big)'.$$
$G$ is solvable if $G^{(k)} = 1$ for some $k$; the least such $k$ is the derived length.

The commutator measures failure to commute: $[x,y]=1$ iff $xy = yx$, so $G' = 1$ iff $G$ is abelian.

blocks.title: The derived subgroup is the smallest abelianising subgroup
blocks.body: $G'$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, the quotient $G/G'$ is abelian, and if $N\trianglelefteq G$ has $G/N$ abelian then $G'\le N$.

Conjugation is a homomorphism, so $g[x,y]g^{-1} = [gxg^{-1}, gyg^{-1}]$: the generating set of $G'$ is closed under conjugation and $G'$ is normal. In $G/G'$ the images satisfy $\bar x\bar y = \bar y\bar x\,\overline{[x,y]} = \bar y\bar x$, so the quotient is abelian. If $G/N$ is abelian, then $xNyN = yNxN$, which says $[x,y]\in N$ for all $x,y$; since $N$ is a subgroup, $G'\le N$.

blocks.title: Solvability through series, subgroups and quotients
blocks.body:
1. $G$ is solvable if and only if it has a chain $1 = G_0 \trianglelefteq G_1 \trianglelefteq \cdots \trianglelefteq G_s = G$ in which each $G_{j}$ is normal in $G_{j+1}$ and each $G_{j+1}/G_j$ is abelian.
2. Subgroups and quotients of solvable groups are solvable.
3. If $N\trianglelefteq G$ and both $N$ and $G/N$ are solvable, then $G$ is solvable.

1. If $G$ is solvable, the derived series read backwards is such a chain, by the previous theorem. Conversely, given a chain, we show $G^{(i)}\le G_{s-i}$ by induction: the case $i=0$ is clear, and since $G_{s-i}/G_{s-i-1}$ is abelian, $G^{(i+1)} = (G^{(i)})' \le (G_{s-i})' \le G_{s-i-1}$. So $G^{(s)}\le G_0 = 1$.

2. If $H\le G$ then $H'\le G'$ and inductively $H^{(i)}\le G^{(i)}$. If $\pi: G\to G/N$ is the quotient map, $\pi$ sends commutators onto commutators, so $\pi(G^{(i)}) = (G/N)^{(i)}$. Both reach $1$ when $G^{(i)}$ does.

3. If $(G/N)^{(k)} = 1$ then $\pi(G^{(k)}) = 1$, i.e. $G^{(k)}\le N$. If also $N^{(l)} = 1$, then $G^{(k+l)} = (G^{(k)})^{(l)} \le N^{(l)} = 1$.

blocks.title: The symmetric groups
blocks.body: Compute the derived series of $S_3$ and $S_4$, and show that $S_n$ is not solvable for $n\ge 5$.
blocks.solution:
In every $S_n$, the sign homomorphism has abelian image, so $S_n'\le A_n$. Also $[(1\,2),(2\,3)] = \big((1\,2)(2\,3)\big)^2$ is a $3$-cycle, and $S_n'$ is normal, so it contains all $3$-cycles (they are all conjugate in $S_n$), which generate $A_n$. Hence $S_n' = A_n$ for $n\ge 3$.

$S_3$: $A_3$ is cyclic of order $3$, so $S_3 \trianglerighteq A_3\trianglerighteq 1$ and $S_3$ is solvable of derived length $2$.

$S_4$: the Klein group $V = \{e, (1\,2)(3\,4), (1\,3)(2\,4), (1\,4)(2\,3)\}$ is normal in $S_4$ and $A_4/V$ has order $3$, so is abelian; thus $A_4'\le V$. $A_4'\neq 1$ because $A_4$ is not abelian, and $A_4'$ is normal in $A_4$. A subgroup of order $2$ of $V$ is not normal in $A_4$ (conjugating by $(1\,2\,3)$ moves $(1\,2)(3\,4)$ to another element of $V$), so $A_4' = V$. Since $V$ is abelian, the series is
$$S_4 \trianglerighteq A_4 \trianglerighteq V \trianglerighteq 1,$$
with orders $24, 12, 4, 1$: $S_4$ is solvable of derived length $3$.

$n\ge5$: $A_n$ is simple and non-abelian, so $A_n'$, a nontrivial normal subgroup, equals $A_n$. The derived series of $S_n$ is stuck at $S_n\trianglerighteq A_n\trianglerighteq A_n\trianglerighteq\cdots$ and never reaches $1$. A group with $G' = G$, like $A_5$, is called perfect.

blocks.title: Nilpotent groups
blocks.body:
The lower central series is $\gamma_1 = G$, $\gamma_{i+1} = [\gamma_i, G]$. The upper central series is $Z_0 = 1$, with $Z_{i+1}$ defined by $Z_{i+1}/Z_i = Z(G/Z_i)$, so $Z_1 = Z(G)$ is the centre. $G$ is nilpotent if $\gamma_{c+1} = 1$ for some $c$; equivalently $Z_c = G$ for some $c$ (the two series reach their ends after the same number of steps). The least such $c$ is the nilpotency class.

Abelian groups are exactly the nilpotent groups of class at most $1$. Each step of the lower central series asks for commutators with the whole group, not just within the previous term, so nilpotency is much stronger than solvability.

blocks.title: Nilpotent implies solvable; $p$-groups are nilpotent
blocks.body:
1. For every $i$, $G^{(i)}\le\gamma_{i+1}$; hence nilpotent groups are solvable.
2. Every group of order $p^n$, $p$ prime, $n\ge1$, has nontrivial centre and is nilpotent.

1. Induction: $G^{(0)} = G = \gamma_1$, and if $G^{(i)}\le\gamma_{i+1}$ then $G^{(i+1)} = [G^{(i)},G^{(i)}] \le [\gamma_{i+1}, G] = \gamma_{i+2}$.

2. Let $P$ act on itself by conjugation. The class equation reads $|P| = |Z(P)| + \sum [P:C_P(x_j)]$, the sum running over representatives of the non-central conjugacy classes. Each index in the sum is a power of $p$ greater than $1$, so $p$ divides every term except possibly $|Z(P)|$; hence $p$ divides $|Z(P)|$ and $Z(P)\neq1$. Now $P/Z(P)$ is a smaller $p$-group (or trivial), so by induction on $n$ its upper central series reaches the whole quotient. Pulling that series back to $P$ and putting $Z(P)$ at the bottom gives the upper central series of $P$, which therefore reaches $P$.

blocks.title: Dihedral groups: always solvable, nilpotent only for powers of 2
blocks.body: Let $D_n = \langle r, s : r^n = s^2 = 1,\ srs^{-1} = r^{-1}\rangle$ be the dihedral group of order $2n$. Show that $D_n$ is solvable, and nilpotent if and only if $n$ is a power of $2$.
blocks.solution:
The rotation subgroup $\langle r\rangle$ is cyclic and has index $2$, hence is normal with quotient of order $2$. Both are abelian, so $D_n$ is solvable by part 3 of the closure theorem.

For the lower central series, compute $[r^a, s] = r^{-a}s^{-1}r^as = r^{-a}r^{-a} = r^{-2a}$, using $s^{-1}r^as = r^{-a}$. Every element of $D_n$ is $r^b$ or $r^bs$, and a similar computation shows every commutator lies in $\langle r^2\rangle$; since $[r,s] = r^{-2}$, we get $\gamma_2 = \langle r^2\rangle$. The next step: elements of $\gamma_2$ are rotations $r^{2a}$; they commute with rotations, and a reflection conjugates $r^{2a}$ to $r^{-2a}$, so the commutators are $1$ or $r^{\mp4a}$. Hence $\gamma_3 = \langle r^4\rangle$, and inductively
$$\gamma_{i+1} = \langle r^{2^i}\rangle.$$
This is trivial for some $i$ exactly when $n$ divides a power of $2$, i.e. when $n$ is a power of $2$. For example $D_4$ (order $8$) has lower central series of orders $8, 2, 1$ and class $2$, while $D_3\cong S_3$ is solvable but not nilpotent: its centre is trivial, so the upper central series never leaves $1$.

blocks.title: A counting argument: groups of order 105
blocks.body: Show that every group of order $105 = 3\cdot5\cdot7$ is solvable, using that groups of order $pq$ ($p<q$ primes) are solvable.
blocks.solution:
First the $pq$ fact: by Sylow, the number $n_q$ of Sylow $q$-subgroups divides $p$ and is $\equiv1\pmod q$; since $p<q$, $n_q = 1$. So the Sylow $q$-subgroup $Q$ is normal, and $Q$ and $G/Q$ are cyclic of prime order, hence $G$ is solvable.

Now let $|G| = 105$. Sylow gives $n_7\mid 15$, $n_7\equiv1\pmod7$, so $n_7\in\{1,15\}$, and $n_5\mid21$, $n_5\equiv1\pmod5$, so $n_5\in\{1,21\}$. Distinct subgroups of prime order meet trivially. If $n_7 = 15$ and $n_5 = 21$, there would be $15\cdot6 = 90$ elements of order $7$ and $21\cdot4 = 84$ of order $5$, more than $105$ in total. So some Sylow subgroup $N$ (of order $5$ or $7$) is normal. Then $N$ is cyclic and $G/N$ has order $21$ or $15$, a product of two primes, hence solvable. By the extension property, $G$ is solvable.

blocks.title: The big theorems
blocks.body:
Several deep results are stated in terms of solvability; their proofs are well beyond this page, but the statements are worth knowing.

- Galois: a polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}$ is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is solvable. The general quintic has Galois group $S_5$, which is not solvable.
- Burnside's $p^aq^b$ theorem: a finite group of order $p^aq^b$, with $p, q$ primes, is solvable. The classical proof uses [[character-theory]].
- Feit–Thompson (1963): every finite group of odd order is solvable. Consequently every non-abelian finite simple group has even order.
- A finite group is nilpotent if and only if it is the direct product of its Sylow subgroups, if and only if every Sylow subgroup is normal. In particular a finite abelian group is the product of its Sylow subgroups, and nilpotent groups behave like "$p$-groups glued trivially".

The smallest non-solvable group is $A_5$, of order $60$; every group of order less than $60$ is solvable.

- The commutator subgroup is generated by commutators; the set of commutators itself need not be a subgroup (although it is in all small examples).
- Extensions preserve solvability but not nilpotency: $S_3$ has normal subgroup $A_3$ with both $A_3$ and $S_3/A_3$ abelian, yet $S_3$ is not nilpotent.
- A nilpotent group is unrelated to a nilpotent element of a ring ($x^n=0$), though nilpotent Lie algebras are related.
- "Solvable" refers to the group, not to any equation it appears in. The Galois group of $x^5 - 2$ is solvable, so that particular quintic is solvable by radicals; only certain quintics, such as $x^5 - 4x + 2$, are not.
- Normality is not transitive: in a series $G_j \trianglelefteq G_{j+1}$, $G_j$ need not be normal in $G$ (in $S_4$, a subgroup of order $2$ of $V$ is normal in $V$ but not in $S_4$).

Solvable groups are the group-theoretic heart of [[galois]] theory and the insolubility of the quintic. The Sylow and class-equation arguments come from [[group-actions]], and Burnside's theorem from [[character-theory]]. In Lie theory the same words describe [[lie-algebras]]: Lie's theorem says every finite-dimensional complex representation of a solvable Lie algebra can be put in upper triangular form, and Engel's theorem characterises nilpotent ones. The finite abelian layers of a solvable group can themselves be described by the structure theorem in [[modules]].

1. Show that the group of invertible upper triangular $2\times2$ real matrices is solvable but not nilpotent.
2. Show that the quaternion group $Q_8$ is nilpotent of class $2$.
3. Prove that every group of order $p^2q$, with $p, q$ distinct primes, is solvable.
4. Prove that if $G$ is nilpotent and $H$ is a proper subgroup, then $H$ is a proper subgroup of its normaliser $N_G(H)$.
