entry.sum: A unique factorisation domain (UFD) is an integral domain in which every nonzero non-unit is a product of irreducibles, uniquely up to order and units, as in $\mathbb{Z}$. Euclidean domains (with a division algorithm) are principal ideal domains (every ideal is generated by one element), and PIDs are UFDs; the ring $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$, where $6 = 2\cdot3 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$, shows that unique factorisation can fail.
key: \text{Euclidean domain} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{PID} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{UFD} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{integral domain}
\text{in a UFD (in particular a PID):}\quad p \text{ irreducible} \iff p \text{ prime}
R \text{ a UFD} \;\Longrightarrow\; R[x] \text{ a UFD}\qquad(\text{Gauss})
entry.why: Unique factorisation in rings like the Gaussian integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ turns Diophantine equations such as $x^2+1 = y^3$ into factor-matching problems, and its failure in other rings of integers is what led Kummer and Dedekind to invent ideals.

links.note: A Noetherian domain is a UFD exactly when every height-one prime ideal is principal, and the coordinate ring of a variety is a UFD only when its divisor class group vanishes.
Computer algebra systems compute greatest common divisors and factorisations of polynomials over $\mathbb{Z}$ and finite fields, relying on the fact that these polynomial rings are UFDs.

refs: Ireland & Rosen, A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory

blocks.body:
The [[fta|fundamental theorem of arithmetic]] says that every integer greater than $1$ factors into primes in essentially one way. Many rings beyond $\mathbb{Z}$ are useful in number theory, for example the Gaussian integers $\mathbb{Z}[i] = \{a+bi: a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\}$, and it is natural to ask whether factorisation is unique there too. Sometimes it is, sometimes it is not, and the difference has real consequences for which equations can be solved.

This page sets up the vocabulary (units, irreducibles, primes), proves the chain Euclidean domain $\Rightarrow$ PID $\Rightarrow$ UFD, and uses unique factorisation in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ to solve an equation. It assumes [[rings|rings and ideals]].

blocks.title: Units, associates, irreducibles and primes
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be an integral domain (a commutative ring with $1\neq0$ and no zero divisors).

- A unit is an element with a multiplicative inverse. Elements $a, b$ are associates if $a = ub$ for a unit $u$.
- A nonzero non-unit $p$ is irreducible if $p = ab$ forces $a$ or $b$ to be a unit.
- A nonzero non-unit $p$ is prime if $p\mid ab$ forces $p\mid a$ or $p\mid b$.

In $\mathbb{Z}$ the units are $\pm1$, and the irreducibles and primes are both $\pm2,\pm3,\pm5,\dots$. In general, every prime is irreducible: if $p = ab$ then $p\mid ab$, say $p\mid a$, so $a = pc$, $p = pcb$, $cb = 1$ and $b$ is a unit. The converse can fail, and that failure is exactly what breaks unique factorisation.

blocks.title: Unique factorisation domain
blocks.body:
An integral domain $R$ is a UFD if every nonzero non-unit $a$ can be written as a product $a = p_1p_2\cdots p_r$ of irreducibles, and whenever $a = q_1\cdots q_s$ is another such product, $r = s$ and after reordering each $q_j$ is an associate of $p_j$.

Units must be allowed to move around: in $\mathbb{Z}$, $6 = 2\cdot 3 = (-2)(-3)$ counts as the same factorisation.

blocks.title: A ring without unique factorisation
blocks.body:
Let $R = \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}] = \{a+b\sqrt{-5}\}$ with the norm $N(a+b\sqrt{-5}) = a^2+5b^2$. The norm is multiplicative, $N(xy) = N(x)N(y)$, because it equals $|x|^2$ for the complex number $x$. Consequently $x$ is a unit iff $N(x) = 1$, so the only units are $\pm1$.

Now look at
$$6 = 2\cdot3 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5}).$$
The norms of the four factors are $4, 9, 6, 6$. The equations $a^2+5b^2 = 2$ and $a^2+5b^2=3$ have no integer solutions, so no element has norm $2$ or $3$. If $2 = xy$ with non-units then $N(x)N(y) = 4$ with neither factor $1$, forcing $N(x) = 2$: impossible. The same argument shows $3$ and $1\pm\sqrt{-5}$ are irreducible. None of them are associates (the only units are $\pm1$). So $6$ has two genuinely different factorisations into irreducibles.

The culprit is that $2$ is irreducible but not prime: $2$ divides $(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5}) = 6$ but divides neither factor, since $\frac{1\pm\sqrt{-5}}{2}\notin R$.

blocks.title: Euclidean domain and principal ideal domain
blocks.body:
An integral domain $R$ is a Euclidean domain if there is a function $N: R\setminus\{0\}\to\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ such that for all $a$ and all $b\neq0$ there are $q, r\in R$ with
$$a = qb + r,\qquad r = 0 \ \text{ or } \ N(r) < N(b).$$
$R$ is a principal ideal domain (PID) if every ideal is of the form $(d) = dR$.

Examples of Euclidean domains: $\mathbb{Z}$ with $N(n) = |n|$; $F[x]$ for a field $F$ with $N(f) = \deg f$; and $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ with $N(a+bi) = a^2+b^2$. In each, the Euclidean algorithm (divide, replace the pair by (divisor, remainder), repeat) computes greatest common divisors.

blocks.title: The Gaussian integers are Euclidean
blocks.body: For $a, b\in\mathbb{Z}[i]$ with $b\neq0$ there exist $q,r\in\mathbb{Z}[i]$ with $a = qb+r$ and $N(r)\le\tfrac12N(b)$.

Compute $a/b = x+yi$ in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ and let $q = m+ni$ with $m, n$ the integers nearest to $x, y$. Then $|x-m|\le\tfrac12$ and $|y-n|\le\tfrac12$, so $|a/b - q|^2\le\tfrac14+\tfrac14 = \tfrac12$. Put $r = a - qb\in\mathbb{Z}[i]$; then $N(r) = |b|^2\,|a/b-q|^2\le\tfrac12N(b)$.

blocks.title: Euclidean domain implies PID implies UFD
blocks.body: Every Euclidean domain is a PID, and every PID is a UFD. Moreover, in a PID every irreducible element is prime.

ED $\Rightarrow$ PID. Let $I\neq0$ be an ideal and $b\in I$ a nonzero element with $N(b)$ minimal. For $a\in I$ write $a = qb+r$; then $r = a - qb\in I$, and $N(r)<N(b)$ is impossible, so $r=0$. Hence $I = (b)$.

Irreducible $\Rightarrow$ prime in a PID. Let $p$ be irreducible with $p\mid ab$ and $p\nmid a$. The ideal $(p, a)$ equals $(d)$ for some $d$; since $d\mid p$, $d$ is a unit or an associate of $p$, and the latter would give $p\mid a$. So $(p,a) = R$ and $1 = px+ay$ for some $x, y$. Then $b = pbx + aby$ is divisible by $p$.

Existence of factorisations. First, an ascending chain of ideals $(a_1)\subseteq(a_2)\subseteq\cdots$ in a PID stabilises: the union is an ideal, hence equals $(d)$, and $d$ lies in some $(a_n)$, after which the chain is constant. Now suppose a nonzero non-unit $a$ has no factorisation into irreducibles. Then $a$ is not irreducible, so $a = a_1b_1$ with both non-units, and at least one factor, say $a_1$, has no factorisation. Since $b_1$ is not a unit, $(a)\subsetneq(a_1)$. Repeating with $a_1$ gives a strictly increasing infinite chain, a contradiction.

Uniqueness. Suppose $p_1\cdots p_r = q_1\cdots q_s$ with all factors irreducible. Since $p_1$ is prime, it divides some $q_j$; as $q_j$ is irreducible, $q_j = up_1$ for a unit $u$. Cancel $p_1$ (allowed in a domain) and absorb $u$ into another factor, then induct on $r$. If one side runs out of factors first, a product of irreducibles would equal a unit, which is impossible; so $r=s$.

blocks.title: Beyond PIDs: polynomial rings
blocks.body:
The implications do not reverse. The ring $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a UFD but not a PID: if the ideal $(2, x)$ were $(f)$, then $f\mid2$ would force $f = \pm1$ or $\pm2$; $\pm2$ does not divide $x$, and $f=\pm1$ would make $(2,x)$ the whole ring, yet every element $2g + xh$ has even constant term, so $1\notin(2,x)$. Likewise $F[x,y]$ is a UFD but $(x, y)$ is not principal. There are also PIDs that are not Euclidean for any choice of $N$, the standard example being $\mathbb{Z}\big[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}\big]$.

Why is $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ a UFD? Gauss's theorem: if $R$ is a UFD then so is $R[x]$. We give only an outline of the proof. Call a polynomial primitive if its coefficients have no common prime factor. Gauss's lemma says a product of primitive polynomials is primitive (if a prime $p$ divided all coefficients of $fg$, then in $(R/(p))[x]$, which is a domain because $p$ is prime, we would have $\bar f\bar g = 0$ with $\bar f, \bar g\neq0$). So one can factor in $K[x]$, where $K$ is the field of fractions, a Euclidean domain, and clear denominators without losing uniqueness. By induction $\mathbb{Z}[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ and $F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ are UFDs.

blocks.title: A gcd in the Gaussian integers
blocks.body: Find a greatest common divisor of $11+3i$ and $1+8i$ in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, and write both numbers as multiples of it.
blocks.solution:
Run the Euclidean algorithm, choosing each quotient by rounding the exact quotient in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$.

- $\dfrac{11+3i}{1+8i} = \dfrac{(11+3i)(1-8i)}{65} = \dfrac{35-85i}{65}\approx0.54-1.31i$, so $q = 1-i$ and $11+3i = (1-i)(1+8i) + (2-4i)$.
- $\dfrac{1+8i}{2-4i} = \dfrac{(1+8i)(2+4i)}{20} = \dfrac{-30+20i}{20} = -1.5+i$; take $q = -2+i$: $1+8i = (-2+i)(2-4i) + (1-2i)$.
- $2-4i = 2\,(1-2i)$, remainder $0$.

So $\gcd = 1-2i$, up to the units $\pm1,\pm i$. Indeed $11+3i = (1-2i)(1+5i)$ and $1+8i = (1-2i)(-3+2i)$. As a sanity check, norms are multiplicative: $N(11+3i) = 130 = 5\cdot26$ and $N(1+8i) = 65 = 5\cdot13$, and $N(1-2i) = 5$.

blocks.title: Sums of two squares by factoring
blocks.body: Use unique factorisation in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ to find all ways of writing $65$ as a sum of two squares of positive integers.
blocks.solution:
$a^2+b^2 = 65$ means $N(a+bi) = 65$, i.e. $(a+bi)(a-bi) = 65$. In $\mathbb{Z}[i]$,
$$65 = 5\cdot13 = (2+i)(2-i)(3+2i)(3-2i),$$
a factorisation into irreducibles (each has prime norm $5$ or $13$, so it cannot split further). By uniqueness, $a+bi$ must be a unit times a product containing exactly one of $2\pm i$ and one of $3\pm2i$. Up to units and conjugation there are two choices:
$$(2+i)(3+2i) = 4+7i,\qquad (2+i)(3-2i) = 8-i.$$
So $65 = 4^2+7^2 = 1^2+8^2$, and these are the only representations with $0<a\le b$. The same reasoning gives the general theorem on [[sums-of-squares]].

blocks.title: The equation $x^2+1 = y^3$
blocks.body: Find all integer solutions of $x^2+1 = y^3$.
blocks.solution:
Factor in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$: $(x+i)(x-i) = y^3$.

The two factors are coprime. A common prime factor $\pi$ would divide their difference $2i = (1+i)^2$, so $\pi$ would be an associate of $1+i$. Then $N(1+i) = 2$ divides $N(x+i) = x^2+1 = y^3$, so $y$ is even and $8\mid y^3$. But then $x^2+1$ is even, so $x$ is odd and $x^2+1\equiv2\pmod 8$, a contradiction.

In a UFD, if two coprime elements multiply to a cube, each is a unit times a cube: every prime appears in $y^3$ with exponent divisible by $3$, and all of it sits in one of the two factors. The units $1, -1, i, -i$ are themselves cubes ($i = (-i)^3$), so $x+i = (a+bi)^3$ for some integers $a, b$. Expanding,
$$x + i = (a^3 - 3ab^2) + (3a^2b - b^3)\,i.$$
Comparing imaginary parts, $b(3a^2-b^2) = 1$, so $b = \pm1$. If $b = 1$ then $3a^2 = 2$, impossible; if $b=-1$ then $3a^2-1 = -1$, so $a = 0$. Hence $x = a^3-3ab^2 = 0$ and $y = 1$. The only solution is $(x,y) = (0,1)$.

blocks.body:
- Irreducible and prime coincide in UFDs but not in general: $2$ is irreducible and not prime in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$.
- A UFD need not be a PID ($\mathbb{Z}[x]$, $F[x,y]$), and a PID need not be Euclidean.
- Similar-looking rings behave differently: $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-3}]$ is not a UFD ($4 = 2\cdot2 = (1+\sqrt{-3})(1-\sqrt{-3})$, and nothing has norm $2$), while the slightly larger ring of Eisenstein integers $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$, $\omega = \frac{-1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}$, is Euclidean.
- "Coprime factors of a cube are cubes" needs the units to be cubes too, or an explicit unit factor; in $\mathbb{Z}$ with squares this is why $-1$ has to be handled separately.
- Uniqueness is only up to order and units; $5 = (2+i)(2-i) = (1+2i)(1-2i)$ is one factorisation, since $1+2i = i(2-i)$.

The structure theorem for finitely generated [[modules]] over a PID generalises the classification of finite abelian groups and gives the Jordan form. The arithmetic of [[gaussian-integers]] and [[eisenstein-integers]] rests on their being Euclidean. When unique factorisation of elements fails, as in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$, unique factorisation of [[ideals]] survives in Dedekind domains, and the [[class-group]] measures how far the ring is from being a PID. The finiteness argument with ascending chains is the first appearance of the Noetherian condition studied in [[noetherian-rings]], and Gauss's lemma is also the key to irreducibility tests for [[integer-polynomials]].

1. Show that $3$ is prime in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ but $5$ is not.
2. Prove that in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ the element $3$ is irreducible but not prime.
3. Find $q, r$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ with $x^4+1 = q\,(x^2+x+1) + r$ and $\deg r<2$, and use the Euclidean algorithm to find $\gcd(x^4+1, x^2+x+1)$.
4. Show that $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-2}]$ is Euclidean with respect to $N(a+b\sqrt{-2}) = a^2+2b^2$.

entry.sum: A module over a ring $R$ is what a vector space becomes when the scalars form a ring instead of a field; abelian groups are exactly $\mathbb{Z}$-modules, and a linear operator $T$ on a vector space makes it an $F[x]$-module. Over a principal ideal domain every finitely generated module is a direct sum $R^r\oplus R/(a_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus R/(a_m)$ with $a_1\mid a_2\mid\cdots\mid a_m$, which at once classifies finitely generated abelian groups and gives the rational and Jordan canonical forms.

P A Q = \operatorname{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_k,0,\dots,0),\quad d_1\mid d_2\mid\cdots,\quad d_1d_2\cdots d_j = \gcd(j\times j \text{ minors of } A)

entry.why: One theorem with one algorithm (the Smith normal form) classifies finite abelian groups, computes the homology groups of a space from its cell structure, and produces the Jordan form of a matrix.

links.note: Integral homology groups are finitely generated abelian groups computed by putting the boundary matrices of a cell complex into Smith normal form, which separates the Betti numbers from the torsion.
A representation of a group $G$ over a field $F$ is the same thing as a module over the group algebra $F[G]$, so module theory is the language of representation theory.
The ideal class group of a number field and the group of points of an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ are finitely generated abelian groups, described by the structure theorem.

blocks.body:
In a vector space you can add vectors and multiply them by scalars from a field. Allowing the scalars to come from a ring gives a module. That small change covers a surprising amount: every abelian group is a module over $\mathbb{Z}$ (with $n\cdot g = g+\dots+g$), and a vector space together with a linear operator $T$ is a module over the polynomial ring $F[x]$, where $x$ acts as $T$.

Modules can be far messier than vector spaces, but over a principal ideal domain the finitely generated ones are completely classified. This page states and proves that structure theorem via the Smith normal form of a matrix, then reads off two classical results: the classification of finitely generated abelian groups, and the canonical forms of a linear operator. It assumes [[ufds|PIDs and unique factorisation]] and [[linear-maps]].

blocks.title: Module
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$. An $R$-module is an abelian group $(M,+)$ with a scalar multiplication $R\times M\to M$ such that, for all $r,s\in R$ and $m,n\in M$,
$$r(m+n) = rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m = rm+sm,\quad (rs)m = r(sm),\quad 1m = m.$$
A submodule is a subgroup closed under scalar multiplication; homomorphisms are additive maps with $\varphi(rm) = r\varphi(m)$; the quotient $M/N$ by a submodule is a module in the same way as a [[dual-spaces|quotient space]].

Examples: $R^n$; any ideal $I\subseteq R$ (the submodules of $R$ are exactly its ideals); $R/I$; abelian groups as $\mathbb{Z}$-modules; and $V_T$, a vector space $V$ over $F$ made into an $F[x]$-module by $p(x)\cdot v = p(T)v$.

blocks.title: What changes when scalars cannot be divided
blocks.body:
$M$ is finitely generated if $M = Rm_1+\dots+Rm_n$ for some elements $m_i$, and free with basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$ if every element is uniquely $\sum r_ie_i$, so that $M\cong R^n$. Over a field every module is free. Over a ring, three new phenomena appear.

1. Torsion. In the $\mathbb{Z}$-module $\mathbb{Z}/6$, the nonzero scalar $6$ kills every element. An element $m$ is torsion if $rm = 0$ for some nonzero $r$; torsion elements can never be part of a basis, so $\mathbb{Z}/6$ is not free.
2. Independent sets need not extend to bases. In $\mathbb{Z}$, the single element $2$ is linearly independent but no basis of $\mathbb{Z}$ contains it.
3. Generating sets need not shrink to bases. $\{2, 3\}$ generates $\mathbb{Z}$, yet neither element alone does, and the pair is not independent ($3\cdot2 - 2\cdot3 = 0$).

Over a PID the damage is limited: one can prove that every submodule of $R^n$ is free of rank at most $n$ (by induction on $n$, projecting onto the last coordinate, whose image is an ideal and hence principal). In particular submodules of finitely generated modules are finitely generated.

blocks.title: Smith normal form
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be a PID and $A$ an $m\times n$ matrix over $R$. There are invertible matrices $P$ ($m\times m$) and $Q$ ($n\times n$) over $R$ with
$$PAQ = \begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_k) & 0\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix},\qquad d_1\mid d_2\mid\cdots\mid d_k,\ d_i\neq0.$$
The $d_i$ are unique up to units: $d_1d_2\cdots d_j$ is the gcd of all $j\times j$ minors of $A$, and $k = \operatorname{rank}A$.

blocks.title: Proof for a Euclidean domain
blocks.body:
Use three kinds of invertible row and column operations: swapping two rows (or columns), multiplying one by a unit, and adding a multiple of one row (column) to another. Each is multiplication by an invertible matrix on the left (right).

If $A = 0$ we are done. Otherwise move a nonzero entry of smallest norm to position $(1,1)$. Divide every other entry of the first column by it: $a_{i1} = qa_{11}+r$; subtracting $q$ times row $1$ from row $i$ leaves $r$. If some $r\neq0$, it has smaller norm than $a_{11}$; move it to the corner and start again. Since norms are non-negative integers this cannot go on forever, so eventually the first column, and likewise the first row, are zero apart from $a_{11}$. If some other entry $a_{ij}$ is not divisible by $a_{11}$, add row $i$ to row $1$ and repeat; the remainder of $a_{ij}$ again lowers the corner norm. We end with $a_{11}$ dividing every remaining entry, and induct on the smaller block, whose entries stay multiples of $a_{11}$. (For a general PID, replace each division step by a Bézout step: if $g = \gcd(a,b) = sa+tb$, the invertible matrix $\begin{pmatrix}s&t\\-b/g&a/g\end{pmatrix}$ sends the column $(a,b)$ to $(g,0)$; the number of prime factors of the corner entry then plays the role of the norm.)

Uniqueness: an elementary operation does not change the ideal generated by the $j\times j$ minors (each new minor is a combination of old ones, and the operation can be reversed). For the diagonal matrix that ideal is generated by $d_1\cdots d_j$, using the divisibility chain.

blocks.title: Structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be a PID and $M$ a finitely generated $R$-module. Then
$$M\cong R^r\oplus R/(a_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus R/(a_m)$$
for some $r\ge0$ and nonzero non-units $a_1\mid a_2\mid\cdots\mid a_m$. The rank $r$ and the ideals $(a_i)$, the invariant factors, are uniquely determined by $M$. Splitting each $a_i$ into prime powers by the [[crt|Chinese remainder theorem]], $R/(p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_t^{e_t})\cong R/(p_1^{e_1})\oplus\cdots\oplus R/(p_t^{e_t})$, gives the equivalent elementary divisor form, a sum of $R^r$ and cyclic modules $R/(p^e)$.

blocks.title: Proof of existence, and outline of uniqueness
blocks.body:
Choose generators $m_1,\dots,m_n$ and let $\pi: R^n\to M$ send $e_i\mapsto m_i$. Its kernel $K$, the module of relations, is a submodule of $R^n$, hence finitely generated; write its generators as the rows of a matrix $A$. Then $M\cong R^n/K$, where $K$ is the row space of $A$.

Row operations on $A$ change the generators of $K$ but not $K$. Column operations correspond to changing the basis of $R^n$, which replaces $M$ by an isomorphic presentation. So we may replace $A$ by its Smith normal form. With relations $d_1e_1' = 0, \dots, d_ke_k' = 0$ in a new basis $e_1',\dots,e_n'$, the quotient is
$$R^n/K\cong R/(d_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus R/(d_k)\oplus R^{n-k}.$$
Summands with $d_i$ a unit are zero and can be dropped, leaving the stated form with $r = n-k$.

Uniqueness, in outline: $r$ is the dimension of $M\otimes_R F$ over the field of fractions $F$ of $R$ (torsion dies in $F$), and for each prime $p$ the number of $a_i$ divisible by $p^j$ equals the dimension over the field $R/(p)$ of $p^{j-1}T/p^jT$, where $T$ is the torsion submodule. These numbers depend only on $M$.

blocks.title: An abelian group from generators and relations
blocks.body: (a) Identify the abelian group with generators $x, y$ and relations $4x+6y = 0$, $6x+4y = 0$. (b) Do the same for generators $x,y,z$ and relations $2x+4z = 0$, $6y+6z = 0$, $2x+6y+10z = 0$.
blocks.solution:
(a) The relation matrix is $A = \begin{pmatrix}4&6\\6&4\end{pmatrix}$. Subtract column $1$ from column $2$: $\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\6&-2\end{pmatrix}$; swap the columns: $\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\-2&6\end{pmatrix}$; add row $1$ to row $2$: $\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\0&10\end{pmatrix}$; subtract twice column $1$ from column $2$: $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&10\end{pmatrix}$. So the group is
$$\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/10\ \cong\ \mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/5,$$
of order $20 = |\det A|$. The minors confirm it: the gcd of the entries is $d_1 = 2$ and $d_1d_2 = |\det A| = 20$.

(b) Here $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&0&4\\0&6&6\\2&6&10\end{pmatrix}$. The third row is the sum of the first two, so $\det A = 0$ and the rank is $2$. The gcd of the entries is $2$, and the gcd of the $2\times2$ minors is $12$ (for instance the minors $12$ and $-24$ occur, and all are multiples of $12$). Hence $d_1 = 2$, $d_2 = 6$, and the group is $\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/6\oplus\mathbb{Z}$: infinite, with free rank $1$ and torsion subgroup of order $12$.

blocks.title: All abelian groups of order 72
blocks.body: List all abelian groups of order $72$ up to isomorphism, in both invariant factor and elementary divisor form.
blocks.solution:
A finite abelian group has $r=0$, and by the elementary divisor form it is a product of its Sylow subgroups, one for each prime. Since $72 = 2^3\cdot3^2$, the $2$-part is $\mathbb{Z}/8$, $\mathbb{Z}/4\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$ or $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^3$ (one for each partition of $3$) and the $3$-part is $\mathbb{Z}/9$ or $(\mathbb{Z}/3)^2$ (partitions of $2$). That gives $3\times2 = 6$ groups. To get invariant factors, combine the largest prime powers into $a_m$, the next largest into $a_{m-1}$, and so on:
- $\mathbb{Z}/8\oplus\mathbb{Z}/9 \cong \mathbb{Z}/72$
- $\mathbb{Z}/8\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\oplus\mathbb{Z}/24$
- $\mathbb{Z}/4\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/9\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/36$
- $\mathbb{Z}/4\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3\cong\mathbb{Z}/6\oplus\mathbb{Z}/12$
- $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^3\oplus\mathbb{Z}/9\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/18$
- $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^3\oplus(\mathbb{Z}/3)^2\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/6\oplus\mathbb{Z}/6$

In general the number of abelian groups of order $\prod p_i^{e_i}$ is $\prod p(e_i)$, where $p(e)$ is the number of [[partitions]] of $e$.

blocks.title: Linear operators as $F[x]$-modules
blocks.body:
Let $T$ act on $V = F^n$ with matrix $A$. The $F[x]$-module $V_T$ is finitely generated (by any basis) and torsion: by Cayley–Hamilton, the characteristic polynomial kills every vector. One can show that $V_T$ has the presentation $F[x]^n/\operatorname{rows}(xI-A^{\mathsf{T}})$ (the relations are $x e_j - \sum_i a_{ij}e_i$, from $Tb_j = \sum_i a_{ij}b_i$), and transposing does not change the minors, so the Smith normal form of the polynomial matrix $xI - A$, computed over the Euclidean domain $F[x]$, gives
$$V_T\cong F[x]/(f_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus F[x]/(f_m),\qquad f_1\mid\cdots\mid f_m,$$
with monic invariant factors $f_i$. Here $f_m$ is the minimal polynomial of $T$, and $f_1\cdots f_m = \det(xI - A)$ is the characteristic polynomial.

A summand $F[x]/(f)$ with $f = x^d + c_{d-1}x^{d-1}+\dots+c_0$ has basis $1, x, \dots, x^{d-1}$, and multiplication by $x$ has the companion matrix of $f$ in that basis. Putting the companion blocks together gives the rational canonical form, valid over every field. Over $\mathbb{C}$, use elementary divisors instead: a summand $\mathbb{C}[x]/((x-\lambda)^e)$ with basis $(x-\lambda)^{e-1},\dots,(x-\lambda),1$ gives a [[jordan|Jordan block]] of size $e$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$. So the Jordan form is the structure theorem over $\mathbb{C}[x]$.

blocks.title: Reading off a Jordan form
blocks.body: Let $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Find the invariant factors of $xI - A$ and describe $\mathbb{Q}^3$ as a $\mathbb{Q}[x]$-module.
blocks.solution:
We have $xI - A = \begin{pmatrix}x-2&-1&0\\0&x-2&0\\0&0&x-2\end{pmatrix}$. Use the minors. The entry $-1$ is a unit, so $d_1 = 1$. The $2\times2$ minors include $(x-2)^2$, $-(x-2)$ (rows $1,3$ and columns $2,3$), and $0$; every $2\times2$ minor is divisible by $x-2$, so $d_1d_2 = x-2$. The determinant is $(x-2)^3$, so $d_1d_2d_3 = (x-2)^3$. Hence the Smith form is $\operatorname{diag}\big(1,\ x-2,\ (x-2)^2\big)$ and
$$\mathbb{Q}^3_A\cong\mathbb{Q}[x]/(x-2)\oplus\mathbb{Q}[x]/\big((x-2)^2\big).$$
The minimal polynomial is $(x-2)^2$, the characteristic polynomial $(x-2)^3$, and the Jordan form has blocks of sizes $1$ and $2$ for eigenvalue $2$, which is what $A$ already is. By contrast, $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ gives the single summand $\mathbb{Q}[x]/(x^2+1)$: since $x^2+1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$, there are no eigenvectors and no smaller invariant subspaces.

blocks.body:
- $\mathbb{Z}/6\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3$ because $2$ and $3$ are coprime, but $\mathbb{Z}/4\not\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$ (the first has an element of order $4$).
- Invariant factors must form a divisibility chain; $\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3$ is written as $\mathbb{Z}/6$ in invariant factor form, not as two factors.
- Finite generation matters: $\mathbb{Q}$ is a torsion-free $\mathbb{Z}$-module that is not free (any two rationals are dependent over $\mathbb{Z}$, but $\mathbb{Q}$ is not cyclic). For finitely generated modules over a PID, torsion-free does imply free.
- The PID hypothesis matters: the ideal $(2,x)$ of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a torsion-free $\mathbb{Z}[x]$-module that is not free, since any two elements $f, g$ satisfy the relation $g\cdot f - f\cdot g = 0$ while one element cannot generate it.
- Row operations change the relations but not the module; column operations change the generators. Both are allowed, but only invertible ones over $R$: over $\mathbb{Z}$ you may not divide a row by $2$.

Modules over rings that are not PIDs are studied in [[noetherian-rings]], where finite generation of submodules is built into the definition. The $F[x]$-module viewpoint explains [[jordan|Jordan form]] and the minimal polynomial; modules over a group algebra are [[group-representations]]; and [[tensor-products]] of modules extend the construction for vector spaces. Smith normal form over $\mathbb{Z}$ is the standard algorithm for [[homology]] groups, and the structure theorem for $\mathbb{Z}$-modules describes the finite abelian [[groups]], the [[class-group]] of a number field, and the Mordell–Weil group of an [[elliptic-curves|elliptic curve]].

1. Find the invariant factors of the abelian group with generators $x,y$ and relations $6x+9y = 0$, $12x+6y = 0$.
2. How many abelian groups of order $10^5$ are there up to isomorphism?
3. Show that $$\mathbb{Z}/m\oplus\mathbb{Z}/n\cong\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(m,n)\oplus\mathbb{Z}/\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)$$.
4. Two $3\times3$ complex matrices have the same characteristic polynomial and the same minimal polynomial. Must they be similar? What about $4\times4$ matrices?
